items.excerpt: 桑田佳祐が、ライブアルバム『九段下フォーク・フェスティバル’25』を2026年11月3日（火・祝）にリリースする。 2025年、放送30周年を迎えたレギュラーラジオ「桑田佳祐のやさしい夜遊び」と開局55周年を迎えたTOKYO FM。この2つの周年を記念し、2025年10月12日に日本武道館にて〈九段下フォーク・フェスティバル’25〉が開催された。洋邦問わず、ギター1本を持ち寄れば気軽に誰でも楽しめるフォークソングへの愛とリスペクトを込めた本イベントは、桑田が企画発案し、事前告知一切なしであいみょん、桜井和寿（Mr.Children）、竹内まりや、原 由子、吉井和哉（THE YELLOW MONKEY）がシークレットゲストとして登場し、大きな話題となった。 〈九段下フォーク・フェスティバル’25〉ロゴ

items.album: walakos ~ baseline distortion
items.excerpt: Despite the title, distortion isn’t the defining characteristic of walakos‘s latest. items.body: Despite the title, distortion isn’t the defining characteristic of walakos‘s latest. Much of the production is remarkably lucid, leaving enough space around the low end and harder electronic textures for small changes in timbre and rhythm to register. “Sapphire” establishes this physical vocabulary, while “Link State” opens it out, playing with depth and distance. “Recursion Error” is more nervous and insistent, its recurring rhythmic figures subtly displaced and reshaped as the track progresses. The collaborations broaden that vocabulary. “Ray” features guitar from Maksym Borovik (Maxy Force), whose pink Jazzcaster, in walakos’s own words, fills the space in the arrangement. It also gives the track a looser rhythmic character, with syncopated layers producing an elastic, slightly off-centre groove. “-RWD” reaches further into walakos’s personal history. It incorporates samples from earlier jams with his friend Mykyta Troiepольskyi (mutedbirds), a previous collaborator on “Wyciczone ptaki” from Interrupted. Old sounds resurface within a hazier, more melancholic piece, driven by a digitally treated voice that slips in and out of the surrounding texture. “1,74B COP” brings a very different voice into the album. A Colombian mother asking for news about her son serving in the Ukrainian military cuts through the electronic patterns. This creates a distancing effect giving the track an unexpected documentary weight. It is also a reminder that walakos is one half of warнякання with Anton Slepakov, a project that has produced one of the most effective ongoing chronicles of the full-scale invasion. What began as an attempt to register the war from the perspective of civilians living through it has inevitably changed as both Slepakov and walakos have since joined the Ukrainian military, shifting the project’s vantage point from life under invasion to the experience of those now serving within the war itself. The closing “Pixel (im)perfect” gathers clicks, pulses and synthetic fragments into a buoyant groove, punctuated by brief vocals and the return of the digitally treated voice heard earlier in the album. It makes for a fitting ending: busy, playful and still moving forward. Even when the music becomes melancholic or emotionally charged, baseline distortion keeps searching for movement. There is a tone of vintage in its sound but without the nostalgia. Rhythms change shape, layers thin out pulling details into focus and new variations flourish. The album is released by Dnipropop, a label that continues to function as a focal point for the city’s scene and artists orbiting beyond it. Walakos’s own note accompanying the album perhaps provides the more important context: he thanks the Ukrainian music community for continuing to make music, support one another and keep the ecosystem alive “despite all the circumstances”, dedicating his respect to those defending the country and remembering those still serving. photo by Roksolana Deineha To help us breakdown the production process of baseline distortion, I approached walakos directly. We have been in direct contact since I first interviewed him for the Ukrainian Field Notes series and it is always a pleasure and a privilige to get to speak to him. The liner notes describe baseline distortion as music written after “the familiar conditions of life had already changed”, with the title referring to a change in the basic frameworks through which you perceive the world. Musically, though, the album is very precise and rhythmically grounded, often establishing a stable groove and then altering what happens around it. What does “baseline distortion” mean to you, and did that idea influence the way you approached rhythm and structure on the record? “Baseline distortion” is a scientific term describing when an instrument’s readings begin to deviate from the norm under the influence of stimuli that are atypical for the sensor. Yes, our baseline settings have changed as well. It’s not just me, but I very often draw on my personal experience to interpret it through music. At first, one might think of constant stress, sleep deprivation, anxiety, and PTSD. But you say the tracks have become clearer and more balanced. And that, too, is baseline distortion. We all wanted a freer, more relaxed, and easier life. But times don’t let us choose. They dictate their own terms. And just like the approach to creating tracks—that’s exactly how the life of a civilian, who was supposed to become a soldier, ultimately transforms. More discipline, more clarity, more obedience. In music, this manifests in crisp grooves and adherence to a specific style. Before, I could afford to “blur” my musical vision and approach to production, but now I can’t. And I think this is an honest interpretation of my storytelling. Compared with Interrupted, there is a stronger pull towards UK club music here, but you rarely settle into a straightforward genre vocabulary. “Sapphire”, “Link State” and “Recursion Error” maintain recognisable rhythmic grids while constantly shifting accents and textures, while “Ray”, with Maksym Borovyk on guitar, opens up a much more spacious harmonic field. What drew you towards this UK-influenced rhythmic language, and how did the collaborations with Borovyk and Mykyta Troepolsky affect the direction of the album? Here, the general concept is followed. A soldier has a sphere of obedience, a sphere for interpreting orders, and personal aspects that you won’t lose no matter what. All of this is reflected in the music: there’s the “order” of the style, your interpretation of the “assigned task,” and the personal elements that keep you grounded in all of this and remain constant. Accordingly, the UK dictates the style (yes, I genuinely love and submit to it), and there’s room for interpretation through textures and accents. But all of that is just the “frame,” and there has to be a precious gem that you set into it: whether it’s a sample from a jam session with a friend that’s dear to your heart, or a melodic ambient guitar track with a shimmer from a buddy with whom you’re always joking around and almost never have a heart-to-heart. And that’s his very sincere voice. In “1,74B COP”, we suddenly hear the voice of a Colombian woman saying in Spanish that she is worried, wants to speak to her son and hasn’t heard from him for some time. Given that Colombians have travelled to fight on both the Ukrainian and Russian sides of the war, the recording introduces a disturbing ambiguity into the track. Where did you find it, who is the woman trying to contact, and what made you place this particular voice in “1,74B COP”? This is the most heart-wrenching part of the release. I’ve previously worked with this particular group of soldiers in the Ukrainian army. I have the utmost respect for these men. I’ve had deep conversations with some of them and continue to stay in touch even after they’ve been wounded or returned home. I was struck by these experienced men who led orderly, comfortable lives, who flew halfway across the globe because they couldn’t stand by and watch the injustice unfolding here. They shared my contact information with their loved ones, describing me as someone they could trust. Sometimes the mothers and wives of soldiers would call me, often in the middle of the night (since we’re in different time zones), asking about their well-being, even after I had already left my previous unit. As an empathetic person, I keenly felt the full range of emotions and struggles of a mother who, for a variety of reasons, couldn’t speak with her son. This voice is a symbolic representation of all the mothers waiting for their sons. I salute all the foreign soldiers who are helping us defend our land. As for the sample: I feel it would be unethical to use a recording of a private conversation, but I was able to convey the general meaning using modern synthesis. painting by Roksolana Deineha The album artwork depicts the painting Lost by Roksolana Deineha. What made you go for that image in particular? The painting is framed and hanging in our home. It has a very specific mood: danger, alertness, confusion, determination. I thought about the cover for quite a while; I even briefly considered going with the aesthetic of scientific instruments and their distortions. In the midst of this agonizing decision, we were talking with Roksolana — she asked me point-blank, “Describe what your album is about.” I described the moods and themes that guided me. Then she said, “Look at the wall. It seems like the guy in the painting knows what you’re talking about.” That’s when I stopped looking for another visual. You are currently serving in the Ukrainian military, while warнякання, your ongoing project with Anton Slepakov, confronts the experience of war much more explicitly through Anton’s words and your electronic compositions. baseline distortion comes out of the same changed reality but largely avoids verbal narrative. How has serving in the military affected your ability and desire to make music, and do walakos and warнякання now provide you with different ways of processing what you are living through? To be honest, war offers the living one gift amid the overwhelming horror, death, and destruction. A keener sense of life itself. Enjoying a cup of coffee, hugging a loved one, or passionately doing what you love. How does living under conditions of highly probable death affect me? In the same way. I want to drink in this life in big gulps: to greet the dawn, to see my parents, to drink coffee with friends, to create music… And yes… In warнякання, Anton’s voice truly sets the overall tone, and from that, I build music that serves as a framework and support for the stories Anton unfolds. This duo allows us to view our shared present through Anton’s eyes and highlight it. In my own project, there’s only my life, my stories, and my storytelling which shapes and determines the artistic expression of the tracks. There are plenty of stories in my life, which means there’s plenty of color for the musical canvas. I conceptualize the chosen stories, select the “musical colors,” and write the composition. That’s why even under similar circumstances the musical interpretation differs slightly. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Kid Bucle, either knowing or unknowingly, takes a lineage built from futurism, tek-funk, broken machinery and the pleasure of the unexpected, then subjects it to contemporary pressure until something new and now begins to emerge. Contemporary electronic art: vast, physical and breathtakingly detailed Incompleteness by Kid Bucle   I have humbly decided that this extended player affords me a slightly self-indulgent opportunity to locate myself within a lineage of which I can only ever claim to be a fragment. Or at least, the Incompleteness is so good, it’s triggered a reflective expression. Regardless, here we are. By the latter half of the 1990s, the UK underground party scene had become a sprawling ecosystem of overlapping futures. We were listening and dancing to top-tier releases from Underground Resistance, Jeff Mills, Transmat, Aril Brikha, The Jedi Knights, Dave Angel and, inevitably, Aphex Twin; elsewhere tracing the Detroit lineage through artists such as Drexciya, Dopplereffekt, Stasis et al, while the years around the turn of the century brought everything from Legowelt to LA Synthesis. Ian O’Brien, and Swayzak into our mixes. Alongside all this, an apparently endless procession of mutations and crossovers moved between techno(s) and house(s)—much of which would later be flattened, retrospectively packaged and homogenized beneath the convenient umbrella of tech house. But our lived reality was considerably less tidy than the history books might suggest. Genres were still adventurous and porous. Scenes were still arguing with themselves. New sounds arrived before anyone had decided what to call them. And beneath the increasingly polished surface of the decade’s mainstream culture, something else was happening. The countercultural and artistic momentum inherited from earlier generations had not disappeared; it had dispersed. As the millennium approached—with all the absurdly romantic anxiety of a fabricated timestamp promising either technological transcendence or digital collapse—another current began to gather force. For those of us becoming desensitised to the necessary but increasingly familiar four-to-the-floor grammar of house and techno, another possibility was emerging: a renewed electro futurism that felt less like revival than reactivation. There were already telling fractures in the beat. Breakbeat had changed the landscape. Broken beat, trip hop and electronica had widened the vocabulary. And when we went out, we wanted something fast, digital, electronic and funky enough to make the body move without requiring it to march. Something that excited the central nervous system and that spoke to the parameters of our escapist fugue states. UR003 was a mainstay. “Incompleteness doesn’t feel incomplete because of any lack. It feels beautifully. incomplete because it understands that electronic music itself is unfinished—that the machine still contains possibilities not one of us has properly accessed yet.” ~Will Wonks Such electro became cool again because, for a while, it seemed to offer an escape from the routine of clubbing routines. The second generation unwittingly arrived carrying the DNA of the pioneers but operating within a newly expanded electronic landscape. Carl Finlow. Anthony Rother. Sons of Slough. Scopex Records. Tipper. Spacetime Continuum all flirted with or championed nu-skool electro. As well as a million other unsung operators, each extending and corrupting the signal. Their work reimagined the pioneering futurism of Kraftwerk alongside the electro-funk detonations of Bambaataa, Hashim‘s Al-Naafiysh, Juan Atkins‘ Cybotron and Soul Sonic Force, YMO, Thomas Dolby, Moroder, and on. The result was not a revival. It was a reprogramming: a music that understood its ancestry while refusing to remain obedient to it. And that mattered because the consequences extended far beyond electro itself. That late-90s emergence contained the seed of the genre hybridisation we now take for granted: the willingness to let one vocabulary contaminate another, to treat genre less as a boundary than a component. Twenty-five years later, the descendants are everywhere. From glitch, Vapourwave, Chiptune, and experimental sound design pursued almost for its own sake, through braindance and Drill into the innumerable hybrid forms that followed, the electronic underground has become increasingly less concerned with preserving distinctions than discovering what happens when those distinctions are deliberately ignored. Of course, in the end there are not really two seasons of electro music—before and after, old and new. There is only the thread and the evolutionary impulses across it. A single, constantly mutating continuum that survives precisely because it is repeatedly pulled apart and reassembled as we explore, as we progressively commit to a healthy artistic development, backed up against an almost cataclysmic regression as a total species. That evolutionary thread remains alive now in the work orbiting labels such as CPU, Frustrated Funk, Analogical Force, Lunar Disko, Semantica; artists such as Annie Hall, Fleck E.S.C., Plant 43, Scape One, and here, the numerous entrants within the Science Cult ecosystem—my apologies to the innumerable others omitted here in the interests of eventually getting to the point. What connects them is not simply a sound. It is a commitment to beats and textures as an ongoing unfinished technology; to the idea that electronic music can still be strange, physical, funny, brutal, sophisticated and forward-facing all at once. That it remembers its roots as we subjectively forget. Any sufficiently deep study of art eventually reveals two competing pulses within the creative whorl. One is inheritance: the necessity of what has come before, its vocabulary and accumulated possibilities. The other is departure: the impulse to misuse that vocabulary in order to discover what else it might become. Both are necessary because both ultimately serve the same purpose—to express what is, right here, right now. Then there are the anomalies. The pioneers who, for a brief period at least, appear to operate without discernible reference points; artists whose internal cosmology is so singular that influence becomes difficult to map until everybody else catches up. Aphex Twin is an obvious example for our purposes. Such figures are rare. They are timestamps rather than trends. Archetypes, if you like: creative appearances through which something enters the culture and leaves a mark durable enough to outlive its moment. It is not for me to say here whether Kid Bucle (aka Valencia, Spain-based Malsum — Ibrahim Pedernera Martinez) belongs amongst such company. Nor, really, is it the job of a review to make that kind of proclamation. No objective assessment can supersede direct subjective experience. But perhaps one purpose of this indulgent preamble is to establish the territory into which this Incompleteness release newly arrives—and to make it absolutely clear that the effort being expended here is inspired entirely by the music itself. Because finally, this is about the music. Nothing else. Incompleteness then, is a forward-facing kick in the proverbial: a prototypical experimental experience that moves in, out, around and through what we might loosely describe as electro’s most progressive potential. It does so without sounding particularly interested in protecting the borders of electro in the first place. There is a bias towards increased tempo and a natural disposition towards the collapse of genre itself—for want of a better term, post-genre. The constituent elements of electronic music are all present, but they have been liberated (obliterated?) from their traditional obligations. Tops and bottoms. Breadth and depth. Width and height. Rhythm, texture, melody and impact are scattered across the stereo field like components from several different machines forced to cooperate. The programming is scattergun, intricate and frequently exhilarating. The digi-breaks are unapologetically funkapolian. Yet beneath the technical complexity lies an innate musicality: atmosphere, timbre and cinematic texture are not decorative additions but structural components. This is music with a stank-faced sense of awe about it. One listen’s partly in admiration and partly in disbelief that someone has managed to keep so many moving parts from tearing the entire thing apart, whilst still landing in majesty and beauty. Art that hits the spot in the listener it appeared at in its creator. “Parasitos” opens the EP with precisely that tendency towards atmosphere. Broken electronic architecture stutters and strafes, evolving and mutating through vaguely Eastern folk motifs, tearing bass and binary science. Dust-and-musk textures collide with braindance-adjacent chopped Amen snares, occasionally summoning the restless imagination of early (Sony) Tipper without ever settling into anything near imitation. It is a beautifully brutal dalliance between effort and instinct, a near-perfect amalgam of technical obsession and artistic purpose. This is an electronic wonk at work inside the digital framework of contemporary electronic production—and every decision appears to have enduring consequences. “Space Feedback” is something else again. Nothing feels absent. Nothing feels superfluous. Every bolt and bough appears to have been considered, as though a bomb is being meticulously dismantled, tenderly rebuilt and then deliberately detonated anyway. It is perhaps the purest embodiment of everything this review is struggling to describe with far too many words. Broken electro structures buckle against stuttering, hard-funked woob bass; summer-warm pads provide unexpected emotional oxygen to create clean air between the mechanical clanks and insectoid impacts. The sheer finesse here is delicious. Music more than worth the cost to both composer and audience. This is, arguably, quite simply, a classic in waiting. Title track, “Incompleteness,” opens with something approaching a Villeneuve-ian majesty. Monumental synth grandeur and bubbling acid stabs occupy an immense cinematic space before the next wave of thundering rhythm begins to tenderly pound both inside and outside the implied loop. Formation and collapse coalesce in abandon. Systems establish themselves only to be interrupted by their own malfunction. It is difficult not to hear the labour in the work—not in the sense of something overworked, but because the time, technique and attention are inscribed directly into the sound. Whether innate or learned is beside the point. The skill is unapologetically on display. It is an extraordinary piece of contemporary electronic art: vast, physical and breathtakingly detailed. “Decipher” takes the closing-credits position and, true to the spirit of the EP, refuses merely to repeat what has gone before. The opportunity to say something different—to demonstrate range, shade and alternative possibility—is grasped with both hands. Thundering, rolling tribal rhythms rumble beneath high-octane strings and expansive pads, while percussive refrains and double-time synthesizer arpeggios build further cinematic dimensions around the forming rhythms. There is a wonderful sense of musicality here, almost of scoring: the feeling that the music is accompanying images we have not yet seen. And perhaps that is the achievement of Incompleteness as an apparently single release set among the routines of too many others. It understands the continuum without becoming trapped by it. Its references are not a museum of influences but raw material. The past is present only insofar as it can still be made useful. Kid Bucle, either knowing or unknowingly, takes a lineage built from futurism, tek-funk, broken machinery and the pleasure of the unexpected, then subjects it to contemporary pressure until something new and now begins to emerge. There is rare bravery in that. There is serious technique. More importantly, here there is absolute joy. The glory of art in full effect. Incompleteness doesn’t feel incomplete because of any lack. It feels beautifully. incomplete because it understands that electronic music itself is unfinished—that the machine still contains possibilities not one of us has properly accessed yet. This EP is an unequivocal 10/10 proposition. Incompleteness is available on Science Cult. items.body: For the fourth episode of our Musical Road to WOMEX, we head to a village room in southern Taiwan, where a group of Paiwan elders usually gather to sing their own folk songs. Into that room, one afternoon, walked a young metal drummer who had just moved home. Sauljaljui was back in Kapanan, her village in the Hengchun peninsula at Taiwan’s southern tip. Behind her were the university years, a nu-metal band, and a pile of rejected applications to Spring Scream, the festival every Taiwanese underground musician dreams of playing. She mentioned to an auntie that she still wanted to make music. The auntie said she knew somewhere… Old people’s music, she thought when the door opened onto a dozen elderly villagers with yueqin in their laps, the two-stringed Chinese moon lute, working through Paiwan songs she had never bothered to learn. She stayed anyway, pulled up a cajón, started holding the rhythm for them, and found they sang steadier for it. Soon she was playing every session, then performing with them, and they began treating her as one of their own grandchildren. It was only then, deep into that company, that she thought to ask one of the old women what she was actually singing about, and got back a memory from the woman’s childhood: a flower she’d spotted high on a cliff while playing hide-and-seek, too far up to pick, so she just stood and looked at it until the spring wind carried its scent down to her. She has said she felt ashamed and warmed at once. Folk music, it turned out, could be a way of singing the land itself, and she had been sitting in the room where it happened without hearing it. So she stopped keeping time for the elders and started learning from them, taking up the yueqin alongside the children of the village. Two strings, an instrument that had never belonged to her people, and somehow enough: she found her own idiom inside those constraints, folding in Austronesian rhythms gathered on tour and playing the lute as a rhythm section rather than a melodic voice. She sings mostly in Paiwan, a language spoken by fewer than 200,000 people and outlawed for years under colonial rule. And it was the elders, in the end, who put her on the Spring Scream stage her own band had never reached. That path led out of the village and a long way from it. Her self-produced 2025 album VAIVAIK, a title that means both searching and embarking in Paiwan, took Best Indigenous Language Album at Taiwan’s Golden Melody Awards, and its opening track “Dipin Kari Tang” took Best Arrangement. That one came out of a month she spent living and playing with musicians in Mauritius, and she recorded it with the Taiwu Ballads Troupe back home. She has worked for years inside Small Island Big Song too, which links Austronesian musicians across the Indo-Pacific around the ocean they hold in common. This October she brings all of it to WOMEX in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, another island a long way from Kapanan. Below, she talks about the elders who taught her to sing, about carrying a language most of her audience will not understand, and about what she hopes to find on the island itself. She also curates a playlist of the tracks that shaped her sound, exclusively for Rhythm Passport. You’re bringing music that moved from heavy metal in college to Paiwan melodies rooted in your home village. For a WOMEX audience meeting you for the first time, how would you introduce that journey and the sound it led to? When I moved back to my hometown from the city to work, I met an auntie. I told her that I wanted to start a band and make music, so she took me somewhere. When I opened the door, I was surprised to see that everyone inside was elderly. They were playing the yueqin and singing traditional songs. At that time, I was honestly a little confused, because to me, it sounded like boring “old people’s music.” But after I joined them, I started playing the cajón to accompany them. In fact, with the rhythm of the cajón, they were able to sing together more steadily and in sync. Eventually, I started performing with them and accompanying their songs. One experience that really stayed with me was when we were invited to perform at Spring Scream, one of Taiwan’s most well-known music festivals. It’s a festival that almost every Taiwanese underground band dreams of playing. My own band had applied to Spring Scream many times, but we were never selected. Yet after I returned to my hometown, it was my grandparents from the village who brought me onto that stage. I remember standing backstage and teaching one of the grandpas how to make the “rocker” hand gesture when he went on stage. But when he got up there, he got it wrong and shouted, “Local!” instead. And somehow, the audience went even crazier! (Laughs) One day, I became curious and asked one of the grandmas, “What are the lyrics you’re singing about?” She told me about something that happened when she was a child. One day, while she was playing hide-and-seek, she saw a flower growing high up on a cliff. She wanted to pick it, but it was too far away. So she just kept looking at that flower. When the spring wind came, its fragrance carried into her heart. At that moment, I felt a little ashamed, but also deeply warmed. I realized that folk music could be a way of singing the land itself. As I spent more time with these elders, they began treating me like their own granddaughter. Being around them also made me softer and more gentle as a person. When I sang these songs with them, I felt like I was finally hearing my own true voice. It was as if I had found myself. You’ve said hearing your grandmother sing, a memory of flowers and spring wind carried in the words, changed how you understood what music could do. Does that moment still shape what you want a WOMEX showcase, and a room of strangers, to feel? I hope that when people listen to my music, they can imagine the place where I grew up, the land, the environment, the people, and the culture that have nurtured me. I believe they can hear that my music comes from somewhere real. It carries a kind of life force that has grown directly from the land. You brought the yueqin into Paiwan music by learning it alongside children in your village, even though it isn’t a traditional instrument for your people. Will it be part of what you bring to the WOMEX stage, and what does it let you do that a purely traditional set-up wouldn’t? The yueqin helped me break through creatively. It only has two strings, so there are obviously limitations to what you can do with it. But because of those limitations, I started asking myself how I could express who I am within that restricted space. I began combining the unique melodies of my own culture with the rhythms of Austronesian cultures that I encountered while traveling around the world. Over time, that became my own way of playing. So the yueqin is not just an instrument for me. It has become an important part of my musical language, and it will also be one of the main instruments I use in my performances. VAIVAIK means searching, or embarking, and the album is really about your own journey back to your language and your roots. What do you want a WOMEX audience, most of whom won’t know that story, to understand about that search when they hear it at your showcase? My culture has given me confidence. It taught me to truly believe that “tradition can be invented.” When I became brave enough to respond to my culture with my own ideas, rather than simply following what already existed, I finally felt a sense of openness within myself. It made my soul want to see the world. And now, I want to share that energy with the world without holding anything back. You’ve spoken about your father criticising your Paiwan, and feeling empty after your first award because you didn’t fully understand your own lyrics. Carrying the language to a WOMEX audience who won’t understand a word of it either, does that history change how you’ll sing it? Creating music in my native language naturally comes with its own challenges, especially because we have experienced colonization and the loss of our culture and language. But those difficulties don’t make me feel defeated. Instead, they give me strength. It’s okay if the audience doesn’t understand my language. When I stand on stage, I believe they can still feel the conviction and energy that I carry. Sometimes I think about what the world would be like if there were no language barriers. I believe what would remain is energy. And I believe the energy that my culture has given me can cross those language barriers and allow people to feel that life force. Small Island Big Song connected you with musicians across island cultures of the Indo-Pacific around the shared subject of the ocean. Las Palmas de Gran Canaria is an island too, out in the Atlantic. Is there something about performing on another island, so far from your own, that you’re curious to explore there? I want to learn more about the history, people, culture, and environment of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria. I’m also looking forward to experiencing the place beyond simply being there as a performer. I want to walk through the city, meet the people, and understand how this land lives and breathes. Your records fold Mauritian rhythms and jazz and rock in next to Paiwan tradition. In a WOMEX programme full of the world’s traditions, how do you want that mix to land, and what do you hope people take from your showcase? In the past, when I created music that involved cultural fusion, it was mostly about combining different musical styles. But “Dipin Kari Tang” was different. I lived there for a month, spending every day with local people, living together and jamming together. So this song wasn’t something I imagined from a distance. It came from a real experience and became part of me. In my culture, recognition and belonging can sometimes be more important than blood relations. If we recognize one another, then we are brothers and sisters. That’s the feeling I hope “Dipin Kari Tang” can bring to people. Even if we come from different places and different cultures, if we are willing to recognize and accept one another, we can become family. You’ve said people don’t need to remember your name, only your culture. WOMEX is built around industry attention on individual artists and their catalogues. How do you hold onto that idea in a room like that? I never imagined that one day I would step outside of myself through my music. For me, I’m really just a messenger, a person who carries and shares the things I believe in. And strangely, that gives me a sense of freedom. It’s something that exists on a spiritual level. At the same time, in the commercial world, I hope I can bring these two sides together, the spirit I believe in and my identity as a musician. I am Sauljaljui. I come from the Indigenous people of Taiwan. You wear a lot of different hats, singer, songwriter, teacher, festival organiser with KAPANAN back home. Beyond WOMEX, and maybe thanks to WOMEX, what’s next for you? This year, I bought a new van, and in September I’m going to start a van tour. I’ll be traveling to different Indigenous communities, spending about a month in each one, and sharing how my culture has guided me around the world and influenced my creative journey. I’ve been inspired by many people along the way, so now I want to walk into these communities myself and share what I’ve learned and experienced. I especially hope I can bring new ideas and courage to young people in the communities, and let them know that their culture doesn’t have to be a limitation. It can actually become the strength that allows us to go out into the world. If you could write a short, personal invitation to the people of Las Palmas to come and find your showcase, what would you want them to know before they arrive? I’m Sauljaljui. Your long-lost half-sibling from another mother and another father. Come and listen to what I have to say   This October, Sauljaljui carries the songs of the Paiwan elders who taught her, and the two-stringed moon lute she learned beside them, onto the stage at WOMEX in Las Palmas     PLAYLIST: SAULJALJUJ X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Sauljaljui appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

The mountain she names is home to Horizontes, a village of 195 people at 2,250 metres in the hills northwest of Medellín, where the houses carry their owners’ names on the front instead of street numbers. Vahos’s parents and grandparents lived there, and Sebastián Gómez Agudelo shot the video bet
items.body: “Cuando voy a la montaña, voy a mí“, sings Ana María Vahos on “Nuevos Horizontes”: going to the mountain is going to herself, and to a home unlike anywhere else. The mountain she names is home to Horizontes, a village of 195 people at 2,250 metres in the hills northwest of Medellín, where the houses carry their owners’ names on the front instead of street numbers. Vahos’s parents and grandparents lived there, and Sebastián Gómez Agudelo shot the video between the village and Medellín, following her through the streets and among her family. Born in San Pedro de los Milagros in 1993 and based in Medellín, Vahos writes and performs as a cantautora in a guitar-and-voice format, with the 2022 album Los Días behind her. She sings for El Búho, the recording name of Robin Perkins, who grew up in northern England, studied Latin American Studies in Glasgow, lived in Argentina and Mexico City, and started the label Shika Shika with Argentine producer Barrio Lindo in 2015. “Nuevos Horizontes” is the second single from Hogar, out 18 September on Shika Shika, an album Perkins built around field recordings of his own home life, of travel, of islands and of long evenings with friends. Hogar comes down from Latin focus, the fire in the middle of the house. The word for a home started out naming the fire it was built around. He made the record while putting down roots in France for the first time, and Vahos sings about the opposite journey: home as the place you go back to. Perkins hosts a listening party for the album on 13 September. Listen to “Nuevos Horizontes” HERE and pre-order your copy of Hogar following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: El Búho – Nuevos Horizontes Feat. Ana María Vahos appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Copied from my review at my blog, "Scott's Song by Song Spotlights", where there are links for listening and purchasing.Clicking 5, but really 4.75, nearly perfect, but not quite!The artists on today's album require no introduction for most people who will be reading this. Steve Hackett & Steve Rothery have come together to create an album of instrumental music. Of course, most of you know that Steve Hackett is best known as the lead guitarist in Genesis from 1971-1977, and has had a prolific solo career since 1975, also collaborating with Steve Howe in 1986 in GTR and Chris Squire in "Squackett" in 2011-12. Steve Rothery has been the lead guitarist of Marillion on every album in their catalog plus his solo album "Ghosts of Pripyat" in 2014. Both guitarists are highly respected for their guitar skills and compositional abilities. This album is a decade in the making, with the two coming together when they could at each of their home studios and a studio called The Racket Club. The theme of the album is "the elemental power of the sea". Finally on August 28, 2026, "The Roaring Waves" will be released on InsideOut Records. Rounding out the recordings are:- Steve Hackett / guitar, harmonica- Steve Rothery / guitar, bass, keyboards- Riccardo Romano / keyboards, bass- Daniele Pomo / drums (1-5)- Leon Parr / drums (6,7)I want to thank Oliver Bergmann from Oktober Promotions, and Sharon Chevin for directing me to Oliver. As always, I receive no further compensation, and I call it like I hear it. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Time to check out the music!Track 1 - The Storm (6:50)The track fades in with ocean sounds, then a mellotron string part takes over. A lead guitar melody begins, and a bolero type of rhythm begins to emerge. At 2:17 there is the sound of thunder, and a guitar riff takes the spotlight. The drums and bass are tight. This is ominous, of course, as the track depicts a storm out at sea. The guitar solo at 3:40 sounds like Rothery to my ears, but I have no indication of who is playing what. I believe Hackett took over at around 4:25; but then again, I could be wrong. The guitarists then alternate licks. This is wonderful! At around 6:00 the storm seems to come to an end and things resolve peacefully. Awesome opener!Track 2 - Sandsend (4:46)After a note that fades in, there is a calm moderate tempoed rhythm with the guitarists alternating phrases on the melody. We are in calmer, gently rocking seas now. The synth gets the spotlight briefly at 1:50. This is a nice chill-out piece of music from these guitar masters. In the last minute or so of the track, however. The musical tension seems to build up a bit. Still, it stays pretty calm. Nice track!Track 3 - Red Dragon (4:19)This has a droning, bagpipe-like quality in the intro. When the rhythm section comes in, the tempo is slightly more upbeat. I like the use of controlled feedback. One of the players has a sitar-like tone on the arpeggiated tones. I like the soundscape on this. The tempo double-times at around 2 minutes, briefly. There are a wealth of interesting tones being utilized. The focus is on the music, not the players' virtuosic abilities. Well done; an enjoyable track!Track 4 - The Roaring Waves (7:11)The title track is up next, and the name promises an exciting ride! Hackett (I assume) starts out with an impressive classical guitar bit. An ominous crescendo takes us to an orchestrated keyboard part that establishes the backdrop for the lead guitar. Not sure which one plays what, but I bet it was Steve. Obviously, both players have built a fine reputation for their abilities. The arrangement on this one is more involved than in the previous tracks. I love the crescendo at around 5:00. I like how the two are playing countermelodies at around 5:30. The classical guitar returns to close out this wonderful dynamic track. This one is my favorite, thus far. Track 5 - K-129 (7:52) According to the notes I was provided:Cinematic is right. Songs like the claustrophobic K-129, which details a submarine's final voyage to the bottom of the seabed, dark waters swirling up around it as its crew meet their doom. "You're trying to create an atmosphere", says Rothery. "I came up with the original sequenced sound, and then it's like painting a picture. You have the rhythmical and the melodic and atmospheric elements that you try and construct in such a way to take people on a journey. And it's a fascinating story. Conspiracy theorists think this Russian submarine that went missing at the end of the 60s was trying to start a war between the States and China and that the captain scuttled the ship rather than let them start World War III, incredible."The aforementioned sequence commences the track. Atmospheric guitar tones and occasional drums are peppered over the top. This one is a slow burn. Of course, there are some sonar sound effects along the way to evoke the atmosphere of a submarine. At around 4:14 a steady drum groove begins. The guitarists' lead-lines break some of the musical tension. The rhythm stops before 5:30. A new beat returns just after 6 minutes. The guitar parts are glorious! The track concludes with a single sonar tone. Terrific track. Track 6 - The Black Sea (6:41)According to the notes provided, the (actual) Black Sea is littered with the skeletons of more than 1,000 shipwrecks over the centuries. That will certainly inform the tone of this piece. It begins with a sense of foreboding. There are wonderful clean guitar tones intertwining in the first segment over a gentle 6-8 meter. A melody takes over at around 1:45. The tone of this track is very warm and melodic. There is a sense of forward motion throughout. The two play together at around 5:00 as the music reaches its climax. Afterwards, there is a peaceful resolution. File this under hauntingly beautiful. I love it!Track 7 - Pacific Coast Highway (7:31)Hackett kicks this one off with a bluesy harmonica riff that would make Huey Lewis smile. This one is a fun driving tune! There are even some wordless backing vocals. Hackett's harmonica playing is a noteworthy feature of this track, as Rothery quipped in the info sheet:"And Steve's harmonica on that is so, so good. He said to me at one point, you know, sometimes I think I should have been a harmonica player instead of (a) guitar player."There is still plenty of great guitar playing to be had, though. This one even reminds me, stylistically, of a Joe Satriani tune. This is the one where they cut loose and have some fun! And we as listeners reap the benefits! I like the syncopated riff starting around 5:15. They finally let some shredding licks loose at around 6:10. The final minute of the song has glorious choral music "aahhs". Great ending to a great album.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:I loved it! However, don't expect a proggy flurry of odd-meters and flashy solos. No, this is about the music and creating sound pictures in a cinematic way. The compositions and arrangements are top notch. The production is immaculate. If you are looking for an immersive musical experience, this is the album for you! Of course, it's fun to try to pick out which guitarist is playing what line, it's probably better to forget all of that, and let the music wash over you. I'm giving this a 4.75 out of 5 stars (95%).

items.body: Review by JavierMiranda — Datura Lodge have arrived with something that feels fully formed, confident, and genuinely exciting to listen to, the kind of record that makes you want to tell people about it.The album opens with three tracks, "Mummy", "Stone" and "98 and 94", that flow into each other without a break, and that decision alone tells you a lot about how this band thinks. It works brilliantly. By the time the suite ends you are already hooked, pulled in by the atmosphere and the melodic instinct that runs through everything they do. The arrangements are detailed and rich, with Adam Holzman on keyboards and Ben Karas adding an electrifying violin solo on "Stone", but the melodies are always front and centre, and they stick."Hole" is worth stopping on for a moment. It has that slow-build quality that the best prog tracks share, a patient emotional arc that keeps growing until the guitar solo arrives and just says everything the words could not. There is a Pink Floyd shadow over it that feels completely natural rather than imitated.And then there is "Lodge", which closes the album and is, for me, the best thing on it. It starts with a quiet acoustic passage that immediately brings Genesis to mind, not in an obvious way, just that same sense of stillness and intention. From there it builds into something bigger and more modern, but without ever losing the melodic thread. It is a really moving piece of music.I have played this album a lot and it keeps giving. One of the best progressive rock records of the year. Five stars.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Embroiled by turbulence and tragedy, prog sludge metal masters MASTODON have pretty much ruled theroost in one of prog metal's most gritty subgenres throughout the years since the band's inceptionin 2000 having churned out four classics during their first decade run. While the 2010s may haveseen a dip in quality the band stilled sallied forth into battle delivering solid if not perfectprog sludge metal releases but then change tends to rear its ugly head in unexpected ways and shakesthings up dramatically. After 25 years founding member Brent Hinds succumbed to the tensions brewingin the band and decided to leave the band and then even more shocking died in an unfortunatemotorcycle accident soon after. Would MASTODON continue or call it a day? Given the unevenness andcontinuing decline in quality, many including myself thought it was the end. However that was notthe case. The band not only continued but returns in 2026 with its strongest album since "Crack TheSkye."MARROW DEEP is the 9th album by this Atlanta based act and a turning point in the band's history.Stepping in to fill Hinds' shoes is guitarist / vocalist Nick Johnston formerly of Osmanthus andalso added to team is keyboardist Jo�o Nogueira. A new five-piece version of MASTODON is born. Thealbum also features seven guests adding vocals, bass and percussion including Lamb of God's RandyBlythe and Black Sabbath's Geezer Butcher amongst others. Graced with yet another stylish dose ofalbum cover art that never fails to deliver, MARROW DEEP not only is a pretty album to behold butreally does bring the band full circle to the heavy sludge metal leanings that launched them intopopular favor over two decades ago. After a few wimpy albums during the last decade, the shakeupseems to have reinvigorated the band much like the latest from Neurosis and finds the band inexcellent form not only with stronger compositions but also in musical delivery. While nothing isspectacularly new in the MASTODON universe as far as stylistic approach, everything just sounds morepassionately inspired this time around.Known for their long albums, MARROW DEEP is yet another hour plus crossroads where progressivemetal, sludge metal and stoner rock converge to deliver a lethal dose of filthy sonic grit takingthe band back to the days of "Leviathan" and "Blood Mountain" which happen to be my favorite twoalbums by the band so it goes without saying that this is a much welcome reprise in the band's peakperformances of the early 2000s. The album wastes no time declaring MASTODON is back with avengeance with the opening "Barbarian's Blood" which signals the path to 65 1/2 minutes of 12 sludgytracks that deliver all the MASTODON goods in rich abundance. Steeped with dueling guitar grunge,slower contemplative moments that offer dramatic diversity and the band's uncanny progressivemeanderings, MARROW DEEP is like a big boil that popped and covering your senses with grimy oozethat absolutely reeks! You know, the way sludge metal is supposed to slap you in the face!From the bantering opener throughout there are no weak tracks on this one. Technically the last twotracks, two of my faves are the best. "The Vanishing" offers a doomy intro before erupting intofull-fueled sludgery while "The Three Fates" offers a nice jazzy keyboard break from the brashbravado and despite the presence of keys on this release, they remain fairly subdued and almostundetectable save for scant appearances where they stick out. Overall MASTODON threw the ultimatecurveball in 2026 with MARROW DEEP and along with Neurosis proved that old dogs can still learn newtricks although nothing's really substantially new on this release but rather picking up in a waywhere "Crack The Skye" left off and adding the quality control back to the entire album's playingtime. While i wouldn't call this the band's absolute best, i would call it the best since theirfirst four releases. A stellar year for MASTODON fans it is!

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the earliest Krautrock bands actually began as early as 1964 as the beat group Bentox whichwas founded by the Swiss B�eler twins, Thomas Leidenberger, and Lucky Schmidt and found themselvestouring both Asia and Germany alike however to little financial gain. By 1971 the act grew to aquintet and jumped on the burgeoning psychedelic rock scene known as Krautrock which was takingGermany by storm. With Krautrock you never really know what you're gonna get as sometimes it'sfreaky and folky and other times loud and raucous. As the newly renamed WIND, the band set sail intothe world of psychedelia adopting a plethora of sounds that included not only the kosmische soundsthat were propelled by the likes of Amon Duul II and Guru Guru but the band also looked towards theUK for inspiration drawing some of the heavy psych / early metal moments heard by the likes of UriahHeep and Deep Purple. The band's debut SEASONS showcased these styles set to a heavy psychedelic setting with not only acompetent vocalist but an organ-drenched freakout style of heavier rock with dramatic guitardistortion, fast tempos and even a drummer to keep up with it all. As much proto-metal as lysergic60s psych, WIND also focused on dreamy folk fueled passages and classical excursions making SEASONSa nice varied heady mix into a instrumentally competency seasoned with the psychedelically detached.This band from Erlangen near Nuremberg was apparently seeking a more international acceptance withlyrics in English and nice catchy melodic hooks that kept one foot in the accessible rock paradigmall the while adding the final touches of the more psychedelic Krautrock attributes that the mostadventurous trippers were dishing out in full abundance. The album features six tracks that add up to nearly 42 minutes with the final closing "RedMorningbird" just missing the 16-minute mark. While many tracks are clearly on the heavier sideincluding the opening powerhouse "What We Do Now" and the heavy as a ton of bricks "Dear LittleFriend," other tracks such as "Now It's Over" and "Romance" are more subdued and laced with soaringflute runs and acoustic guitar, touches of jazz and a completely different vibe than the heavierside of the album. The lengthy closer is perhaps the most koschmische expansive progressive piece onthe album with long instrumental drifting, dreaming meditative soundscapes and ethereal nonchalancethrough planet Lysergia although the track eventually bursts into the heavier rock. While many mayfind this album disjointed in its wild mood swings from heavy rockers on acid to well, just plainblitzed out on acid, the ease of how this cast of characters adapts from one extreme to another isactually quite brilliant and for my tastes it all offers a nice varying palette of mood settings.Sounding like Uriah Heep or Deep Purple from a parallel universe, WIND managed to emulate other actsbut really sounds fairly unique in its little in-between zone where heavy psych meets the mosttrippy expansive mediative side of Krautrock. It's actually the perfect album for 1971 which stillshowcased prog as unfinished business that hadn't quite found those formulaic approaches. WINDsuccessfully captured the heavy organ rock aspects that were en vogue at the time as well ascapturing the essence of a true psychedelic Kraut band. Perhaps the closest band i've heard toWIND's first album is another German band, Twenty Sixty Six And Then which released it's classic oneoff the very next year. Overall this is quality progressive heavy psych from 1971 Germany. The banddid release one following album but shed the rock aspects and went full on folk, a move that provedto be the band's undoing but perhaps the comparisons to Uriah Heep were too much and even thoughthis album does remind a lot of that band's earliest prog releases, it's still distinct enough standon its own two feet.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Exploring Birdsong?a genre-blending act featuring Lynsey, who also provides vocals for Lifesigns, Kite Parade, Caligula's Horse, and Espera (the backing vocal group for Sleep Token)?is hailed as a reincarnation of Kate Bush. They also flirt with the style of Meer; imagine a female Einar Solberg with a touch of Leprous. Expect stunning melodies and a modern sound?prog for today that bears a slight resemblance to Kyros."Archipelago" opens with jazzy, soulful piano as Linsey's magnificent voice launches a meltingly beautiful ballad that balances delicacy and sensuality. There is a breathtaking ambient break and a dash of synth-pop?complete with strings and echoes of Meer?before the track shifts into a wild outro. "42" follows with a striking djent riff; it is heavy at its core, yet takes the form of synth-pop/electro-rock. Vocals drive this modern metal track, accompanied by siren-like backing vocals?innovative and effective. "Romanticise" leans even further into electro, featuring 80s-style synth pads that bridge the gap between mainstream pop and new wave. It carries an energetic hint of Sleep Token, building to a soaring, distorted hard-rock climax. "Footprints" is a mid-tempo ballad amplified by backing vocals and Linsey's rising vocal range. Whether segueing directly or not, "Arrhythmia" evokes a conceptual feel, characterized by a gentle tone and the lingering presence of ethereal piano and vocals. A sudden, sultry solo, a searching spoken-word passage, and a measured riff set against backing vocals enchant the space with crystalline harmonics. "Spy In The House Of Love" arrives with the solemn sound of Celtic bagpipes. It features danceable pop keyboards, an infectious groove, and a vibe reminiscent of XTC?it has it all. An 80s throwback explodes in the chorus?an addictive hook that begs to be sung along to."I_You" features subtle undertones of Coldplay; it is quintessential modern pop with a mainstream touch, yet it navigates prog territory with strings and backing vocals that recall Kate Bush. A sonic extravaganza that invites you to headbang. "The Warning" begins with the intimate folk atmosphere of Scandinavian lands; a somber melody cut through by a hard-hitting synth riff, with backing vocals amplifying the intensity. Strings heighten the drama of lyrics questioning whether to stay together or not. A vulnerable vocal performance carries a weight that flirts with decadent gothic styles. The guitars?and eventually the synths?become frenzied; simply sublime. "You Like It Best When It Hurts" follows a similar vein, bolstered by aggressive synths that evoke modern synth-prog. The riff drives forward with a heavy, rapid-fire attack that beautifully blends with ethereal keyboards. That imaginative guitar riff and the vocal harmonies are spellbinding. "Cartography" returns to the band's roots, with echoes of Kate Bush in this romantic piano ballad featuring a divine vocal performance by Lynsey. "Every House We Built" features a synth sound reminiscent of Tangerine Dream. A vocal-led crescendo builds?exploring themes of relationships and guilt?leading to an infectious drop akin to Brian Eno's work, followed by an expressive rise. "Meadowlands" is a ballad that ebbs and flows with the vocals and fresh, sparkling piano. Airy synths guide the track through a "soft-heavy" prog style, building toward a pop-infused chorus featuring the band Meer, culminating in a fiery finale before a cinematic piano outro.Exploring Birdsong delivers a thrilling fusion of pop, rock, hard synth, and progressive music worthy of Meer.(4.75)

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 986Brand X is a British progressive rock band that was founded in London in 1975. Brand X was a jazz fusion band that was active between 1975 and 1980 and had a hiatus from 1980 to 1992. The band was disbanded in 1999 and was reformed in 2016. Brand X is one of the best, most original and well known British bands in the 70's of the jazz/rock fusion scene. Phil Collins formed Brand X in 1975, with Percy Jones, John Goodsall and Robin Lumley. The debut studio album of Brand X, "Unorthodox Behavior" that was released in 1976, presented a band more rooted in the jazz wave than in rock. From that moment, Brand X became an autonomous group, performing live with Preston Heyman on drums instead of Collins, due to his duties with Genesis, although he continued to record with them. Their second studio album, "Moroccan Roll" released in the following year, featured a fifth member, Morris Pert, in addition to Phil.So, "Moroccan Roll" is the second studio album of Brand X that was released in 1977. The line up on "Moroccan Roll" is composed by John Goodsall (backing vocals, electric and acoustic guitars, sitar and effects), Robin Lumley (backing vocals, piano, Fender Rhodes electric piano, autoharp, clavinet, Minimoog ARP Odyssey synthesizer, Roland String synthesizer and effects), Percy Jones (bass, autoharp, marimba and effects), Phil Collins (lead vocals, drums, piano and effects) and Morris Pert (percussion).With their second album, Brand X continued to develop the sound of their debut work "Unorthodox Behaviour". Many of the most familiar elements are still there, like light footed evocative jazz rock with dense textures. However, some new ingredients are also thrown into the mix. As the title itself suggests, the album features, in addition to the jazz rock mix found on their debut album, research and experiments with sounds from the Middle and Far East, mainly from countries like Morocco. So, "Moroccan Roll" delivers a competent jazz rock with small doses of oriental sounds that never make the album boring or tiring. Commercially, the band fared better with this one than with their debut, albeit to a modest extent. Overall, this is an album rated well by the critics and was very well received by the fans of the band."Sun In The Night" is a laid back music, the only one on the album that has words. It sounds neither like Morocco nor like more rock'n'roll. The intensity grows as the song progresses. This is a peculiar, but yet fascinating piece of music. The next two tracks "Why Should I Lend You Mine..." and "...Maybe I'll Lend You Mine After All" move in a completely different direction musically. "Why Should I Lend You Mine" is an excellent instrumental full of surprises ranging from its varied dynamics to the curious percussion and the always virtuous and extended sound of Jones's fretless. Lumley and Goodsall's solos move within an environment where everything seems to levitate. "Maybe I'll Lend You Mine After All" is a brief piece that could well be the coda of the previous one. "Hate Zone" and "Collapsar" complete the A side of the LP. A solo by Collins kicks "Hate Zone" for several seconds. Jones then joins in on the euphoric piece, followed by the rest of the band. This is a very hard grooving track that clearly moves towards jazz rock. The short and spacey "Collapsar" is full of various Lumley's keyboard sounds and takes us down that levitating path for a minute and a half. "Disco Suicide" is an excellent piece, one of the best built on the album. The track is divided into faster and calmer parts that sound a bit different every time they are repeated. Brand X has added vocals for the final segment of this composition. The very short "Orbits" demonstrates the instrumental mastery of Jones with his unparalleled flair and technique. The only instrument on this track is the bass and various effects. The jam session character of "Malaga Virgin" makes this track come closest to the material from "Unorthodox Behaviour". The piece switches between the fast and slow, loud and quiet parts. The interplay is exceedingly virtuosic, especially the solo segments by Jones and Lumley. "Macrocosm" is a celebration of the fusion genre, being intricate and uplifting, a showcase for the individual skills of the musicians. It shows why Brand X has been one of the jazz fusion bands with great relevance for decades.Conclusion: "Moroccan Roll", unlike its predecessor, credits the tracks to individual authors. So, obviously, it's not as jam session based as their debut album. It contains some very interesting musical ideas. The Far East sounds play a very important role. The band presents nine tracks, all of which are fascinating in their own way. From wonderfully calm songs to fascinatingly restless jazz fusion songs with progressive parts, everything is represented with the highest quality. This album ended up being the farewell of Collins, who had to leave since he accumulated the post of vocalist and drummer of Genesis. For those who want to hear developed music with emotion this record definitely offers this perfectly, but if you want the true spirit of Brand X and jazz fusion "Unorthodox Behaviour" is for sure the album to get.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by Stefano61 — There is a particular flatness to Milanese light through the cold months, an industrial grey that tends to reduce ambition to habit and every gesture to the merely reasonable. It is not, on its face, a light out of which cathedrals of sound get built from vibraphone and French horn, harp and string quartet folded into the frame of a rock band. And yet in that grey and reasonable city, at the turn between 1972 and 1973, three young musicians decided otherwise.Alberto Ravasini, Roberto Giuliani and Sandro Lorenzetti formed the first nucleus, carrying between them the vocabulary of jazz clubs and rehearsal rooms rather than concert halls. By the middle of 1973 they had doubled in size, joined by Sergio Lattuada, Maurizio Bianchini and Leonardo Schiavone, whose training had run through classical counterpoint rather than blues scales. The new sextet took the name Maxophone, a word that reads, not unreasonably, as a cousin of saxophone and megaphone, and set about proving that a band built from two opposing musical educations need not choose between them.It took until 1975 for that proof to reach record shops, by which point the golden years of Rock Progressivo Italiano, the years of Le Orme's Uomo Di Pezza and Banco's first two albums, already lay a season or two behind. Sandro Colombini, the producer behind much of Banco del Mutuo Soccorso's early success and many other credits across the decade, brought Maxophone to Produttori Associati, a label built on film scores and jazz sessions that rarely strayed into rock at all. The album was recorded across February, March and April of that year at the Ricordi studios in Milan, engineered by Gaetano Ria, and preceded into the world by a single pairing its opening and third tracks.The cover fell to Cesare Monti, working as always alongside Wanda Monti, the same hand that two years earlier had assembled the notorious collage for Museo Rosenbach's Zarathustra. Where that image courted scandal, this one is content with mystery, and the record inside asks for nothing but attention.What Maxophone built across six songs and forty minutes borrows from everywhere without settling anywhere for long. There is the choral warmth of Genesis in the vocal writing, the keyboard muscle of Emerson in Lattuada's organ runs, the wind instrument menace of King Crimson circa Lizard in Bianchini's horn and Schiavone's reeds, a jazz vocabulary that never announces itself as foreign to the material, and underneath all of it a folk undertow that keeps the whole apparatus rooted in something recognisably Italian. Harp, violin, cello and double bass arrive as guests rather than ornaments, thickening the sextet into something closer to a small orchestra without ever slowing its reflexes.- C'� Un Paese Al Mondo: a piano figure opens onto an imagined country built on ideals of fairness and unclouded truth, sung with a conviction that makes utopia sound briefly plausible, before clarinet, trumpet and a hardening guitar drag the song back toward the actual world.- Fase: the only instrumental here, and the boldest proof of what six formally trained ears can do together, guitar and saxophone trading a nervous energy that resolves, unexpectedly, into forty seconds of vibraphone stillness before the current picks back up.- Al Mancato Compleanno Di Una Farfalla: a classical guitar figure and a flute line that could have wandered in from early Jethro Tull, framing a lyric that hands a fading butterfly's colours forward to whoever comes next, tender where the album's other songs tend toward argument.- Elzeviro: church organ and a voice alone at first, then the leaden weight of the mid seventies pressing in, the image of a man outnumbered and a power already convulsing as it comes apart, before the band answers with one of the record's most searing guitar solos.- Mercanti Di Pazzie: harp and a borrowed phrase from Hindemith's sonata open onto the album's most fragile interior, a dream logic that trades argument for atmosphere and asks to be believed rather than followed.- Antiche Conclusioni Negre: horns and drums in full voice from the first bar, a nine minute survey of everything the band knows how to do, closing on a low choir over solo organ that sounds less like an ending than a valediction.An English sung version followed the same year, with new lyrics credited to a certain J. Bratel rather than straight translations, carrying different titles and a reshuffled running order. It found little of an audience abroad, and history has settled comfortably on the Italian original as the version worth defending.By 1977 the band had time for one more single, Il Fischio Del Vapore backed with Cono Di Gelato, gentler and more modest than anything on the album, and then Maxophone simply stopped. Produttori Associati's brief and uncharacteristic venture into rock had not paid off, the wider scene it belonged to was already contracting around it, and six musicians who had spent years learning to think as one orchestra went back to thinking separately. Schiavone drifted briefly through Stormy Six before settling with the pop group Accademia. All six had already lent their hands, uncredited on the album sleeve but present on tape, to Corrado Castellari's Gente Cos� that same year.It might have ended there, one record and a rumour passed between collectors, had Sergio Lattuada not spent the following decades unwilling to let it. A 2005 box set gathered the unreleased sessions under a title, From Cocoon To Butterfly, that borrowed its own imagery from a five minute song about a fading insect. Three years later Lattuada and Ravasini rebuilt the group around new players, carried it as far as a stage in Tokyo, and in 2017 released a second album carrying words the poet Roberto Roversi had written for them before his own death in 2012. The story closed for good in May of 2018, when Lattuada died and took with him the will that had kept the chrysalis open.What survives on tape from 1975 does not need that later history to justify itself, but it colours the listening all the same. Six players who might easily have spent their careers as session musicians for other people's songs chose instead to spend one album proving what happens when every instrument in the room gets a vote. The sheer plenty of ideas occasionally denies the songs the settled inevitability of the genre's very greatest single statements, and that, rather than any failure of craft or feeling, is the only real argument against calling this an unqualified masterpiece. Everything else argues the other way. Among the crowded company of Italian progressive rock's one album wonders, Maxophone stands close to the summit, and deserves to be met there. My rating: 4,5/5(Bassano del Grappa, Italy, September 2026)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — William D. Drake's solo debut was like reshuffling the deck and starting almost from scratch, though in his case, it is a very special kind of "zero," one rich with nuances that allow for a variety of elements foreign to the Cardiacs' universe to enter the mix. It is a collection of seventeen songs, best described, were it a speech, as "logorrheic", that unfold like tales of life in nature, rural history, mysticism, mythology, and the presence of forests or the sea in English folklore (as heard in the track "The Great Adventurer"). It is no surprise, then, to find Baroque and chamber music accompanying a rock style that is highly artistic yet secular, at once cinematic, psychedelic, and dissonant. From the opening piano notes of "Miaow Miaow," we are instantly transported to another time and place; "Sky in yer Lap" feels like something out of a Shakespearean production, while "Love in an Overcoat" evokes the atmosphere of a cabaret. Throughout the album, the harmonium establishes an antique spirit, one that, in its very antiquity, becomes modern.The track "Paradox" reminded me of John Cale and his piano, evoking something visceral, raw, and stark, though Drake adds repetitive backing vocals that drive the dark, Victorian atmosphere to a fever pitch. There is something hypnotic about "Poor John"; its polyrhythms and trumpet evoke an end-of-the-world orchestra in a medieval city under siege by the plague. Yet, rest assured, "Dragonfly" pulls us away from that scene, transporting us instead to a silent movie screening."Ivy Dun" possesses a level of absurdity...of madness...that makes it one of my favorites; few pieces of music have the power to be so immediate, so direct, it strikes like an invisible bolt of lightning. That chorus and percussion, combined with the piano, don't ask for permission; they simply take hold and keep on reverberating."Lists of Clay," with its organ and deep vocals, is Peter Hammill on The Future Now; it is Gog Magog on In Camera; it is everything right in this upside-down world."Fiery Pyre," with its Eastern flair, reminded me of Siouxsie & The Banshees, while the piano and vocals could easily have been David Bowie; the album is full of nuances, secrets, and hidden compartments waiting to be discovered, each time revealing something new. It is like a labyrinth one never fully masters, despite always being in the same place.Perhaps the place itself is an illusion, a thought that arises while listening to "The Perfect Crime," a track that feels like something straight out of a 1970s Brian Eno record.And it all comes together, Cardiacs, their spirit, and an English past brought into the present with "Quivvy Vivvy." Here, a vaudeville-style format featuring multiple short songs proves the perfect vehicle to convey "Freedom and Love", fittingly, the final, deeply moving track of an ideal debut album, paving the way for several more yet to be discovered.

items.body: Review by sgtpepper — Genesis had left the post-Hackett romantic territory on Abacab though some melodicism from Duke remained (Dodo/Lurker). Genesis embraced more sun and more pop with their eponymous album; though they did it gracefully. Pop songs are well constructed, arranged; they simply have enough to carry on.Phil Collin's vocals have never been better; it's his vocal and then his drums. Kudos to Banks for updating the keyboard sound and style to the New Wave and Synth bands of that time. Fortunately, some trademark Banks' moment remain like the brief instrumental chord sequence in the "Home by the sea" or the colouring on "Taking it all too hard" which features a Yamaha piano.Instrumentally, it's not a feast for all Genesis fans but there's a bit of flesh to cut into - the dense "Just a job to do" which could have easily fit on Abacab. Further, the slowly starting "Silver Rainbow" offers a compensating chorus after the unsuspecting first 90 seconds.Genesis proved to be equally strong in almost any musical setup they stepped in and the shelf labeled "Art pop" fit them well.This is all true if you like any good music including pop (4 stars). If you're a firm art-rock believer or old Genesis fan, consider 2 stars for this album.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It was a strange era, a time of change and readjustment, and one where it was easy to lose one's way. Musicians who wished to stay the course had to confront record labels and even critics who accused them of self-plagiarism; yet, on the other hand, changing direction was seen as an act of betrayal. Nevertheless, Jon Anderson transitioned from making his recording debut as a solo artist to surrounding himself with friends for his second album, Song of Seven, a number that held deep significance for him, symbolizing both the inner quest and a sense of wholeness.The lineup included Dick Morrissey, saxophonist for the jazz-fusion band If; bassist John Giblin (formerly of Brand X); and Morris Pert on drums and percussion, along with, of course, Jack Bruce and Simon Phillips. With this dynamic, groove-laden band, plus additional musicians and a string quartet, Jon handled acoustic guitar, keyboards, and the harp. He composed songs that, while initially striking due to their ultra-modern, early-80s production style (as heard on "For You for Me"), ultimately reveal themselves to be classic Anderson tracks: deeply emotional and reminiscent of his collaborations with Vangelis. It is an epic sound; backed by such solid musicians, the music creates a rich sonic tapestry that colors the scene much like the stained-glass artwork on the album cover. "Some Are Born" is a beautiful acoustic song that could easily have fit into the Yes repertoire had he been recording with his bandmates.There are symphonic touches alongside rhythms that were more contemporary for that era, such as soul, funk, and a bit of jazz (though not the most daring kind). There is something ethnic about "Don't Forget (Nostalgia), something Latin, that is enhanced by John Dankworth's saxophone; meanwhile, "Heart of the Matter," despite its more pop-rock format, is filled with Jon's signature positive energy, and the rhythm section of Jack Bruce on bass and Simon Phillips on drums provides excellent support for the track."Hear It" is a beautiful track, one could easily imagine it within the context of Yes, yet it stands on its own; it embodies Jon's spirit, which possesses a distinct identity of its own, always positive and visionary, inviting the listener to share in that outlook. "Everybody Loves You" has a rhythm that always reminded me of the songs Carole King and Gerry Goffin used to write; I could even picture it on Tapestry. The bass work, along with Morris Pert's percussion, lends the track a warm, jazzy feel, while the arrangement retains a certain complexity toward the end."Take Your Time" is almost a beautiful waltz, enhanced by Giblin's fretless bass and unmistakably Anderson-esque. By the time "Days" arrives, the album has transcended any specific era to become timeless; it features Jon, his guitar, and his signature magic, with minimal keyboard and bass accompaniment, just enough to let the music of his words cast the spell."Song of Seven" is, logically, the title track, and for me, it acts as a counterweight to the rest of the 'lbum, working not in isolation, but as part of the whole. The strings usher in a different atmosphere, one that is more sacred, and mark the point of greatest resemblance to Yes; indeed, at times it is hard to distinguish it from that band, given Jon's unmistakable voice. Rich in melody and character, the song stands tall on its own merits, earning a place among the very best in his repertoire, akin in spirit to the Going for the One era of Yes.A solid album that fits perfectly into the discography and perfectly explains the subsequent trajectory, including further adventures with Vangelis on Short Stories (1980) and Animation (1982), thereby rounding out that concept of wholeness.
