items.body: Synapscape, the German industrial duo of Philipp Münch and Tim Kniep, releases its new album “The Future” on 10 September 2026 through Ant-Zen. The 11-track record arrives on CD in a six-panel digipak and as a digital download. “The Future” mixes mechanical industrial resonance, glitch electronics and rhythm structures rooted in early EBM and downbeat minimalism, then pushes those elements through fractured textures and dark, atmospheric sound treatments. The tracklist runs “Moreish,” “Melting,” “Spring,” “Five Four,” “Dark Alliance,” “Disappear,” “Valley,” “Pick,” “To the Stars,” “Move” and “Work.” The Future by Synapscape The album is the duo’s first full-length since “Still” in 2018, continuing a catalog that Philipp Münch and Tim Kniep have built almost entirely on Ant-Zen, their home label since 1995. About Synapscape Synapscape formed in Bielefeld, Germany, in 1994, when Philipp Münch and Tim Kniep began working together on rhythmic-noise and industrial material. The duo debuted on Ant-Zen with its self-titled album in 1995 and followed it with “Rage” in 1997 and “So What” in 1999, records that paired heavy sequenced beats with noise and power-electronics textures. “Positive Pop” followed in 2001 and “Raw” in 2002, before “Act!” in 2005 and the collaborative “Scenes From a Galton’s Walk,” made with Asche, in 2006. The project continued through “Now” in 2007 and “Again” in 2009, then “Traits” in 2011 and “Rhythm Age” in 2015, moving its sound gradually from early EBM and power noise toward the more technoid, glitch-inflected direction it has kept since. “Still” appeared in 2018 as the duo’s most recent album before the current release. Münch, who also records as The Rorschach Garden and Mandelbrot, discussed his broader catalog in Side-Line’s Click Interview with The Rorschach Garden. “The Future” extends that three-decade run on Ant-Zen with its 10 September 2026 release.

items.body: Swedish synthpop act Split Vision release “Out Of Nowhere”, the first single from their upcoming album “BetaCity”, through Town And Towers Records. The track is an uptempo, melodic synthpop song built on analogue-style synthesizers and sequenced bass lines. “Out Of Nowhere” tells the story of someone who has spent years dealing with sorrow and uncertainty, only to be confronted unexpectedly with a declaration of love: “But suddenly, you whispered in my ear – I want you to love me.” The song marks Split Vision’s first glimpse of the musical direction for “BetaCity”, which the band describes as a natural evolution from their previous release, “Echoes of a New Spell”. Where “Echoes of a New Spell” explored the synthesizers and recording approach associated with early Depeche Mode, “BetaCity” turns toward the early sound of Alphaville, combining warm analogue synthesizers with colder digital textures, wavetable sounds and cinematic synth pads. Split Vision signed with the Scandinavian label Town And Towers Records in 2022 and has since released several singles and EPs; “BetaCity” is planned as the band’s next full-length, on CD and vinyl. About Split Vision Split Vision formed in 1985 in Sweden, when two teenage friends began writing synthpop influenced by Depeche Mode, Yazoo, Erasure and Pet Shop Boys. The line-up grew to four members through high school, and the band played discotheques in North Eastern Skåne in the late 1980s, also appearing on regional radio programmes and talent competitions. In 1988, the single “How Will I Ever” appeared on Platinum Records, followed by a minor Swedish hit with “So Many Times”. The group split up shortly after. Two of the original members, Dan Hansson and Henric Palmqvist, revived Split Vision in 2019, releasing the album “Among the Stars” on 1 October 2020, a record structured around lyrics and soundscapes referencing the cosmos. A music video for the song “Lust”, directed by Norwegian filmmaker Öystein Thorsen, followed in August 2024 and was selected at several international film festivals. Since signing to Town And Towers Records in 2022, Split Vision has released a string of singles and EPs, building toward “BetaCity”, the band’s next full-length album.

items.body: Dismantled are back with new material. Gary Zon‘s electro-industrial project will release the new single “Zero” on 18 September 2026 through Metropolis Records, with a new full-length album set to follow in November. The six-minute track is already listed by digital retailers as a Metropolis release, while the label’s current Dismantled page continues to carry the project’s catalogue. There is considerably more history behind “Zero” than the announcement might initially suggest. The track first surfaced as part of a three-song preview for an album called “Endless”, uploaded to Dismantled’s Bandcamp in November 2021 alongside previews of “Mirror’s Edge” and “Poison”. At the time, the album was expected in 2022 through Metropolis Records in North America and Dependent Records in Europe. The project itself had been announced even earlier. In May 2020, Zon revealed through Metropolis that he was working on an album titled “Endless”, which he described at the time as combining different periods of the Dismantled catalogue into a more cohesive sound, specifically referencing Standard Issue, the self-titled debut and The War Inside Me. That announcement accompanied “No Escape”, a track written during the early months of the pandemic. Six years later, a current retail listing gives “Endless” a 20 November 2026 release date on CD, with the catalogue number/EAN 0782388148320. Metropolis has not yet published a complete 2026 album page, tracklist or detailed production credits, so those details remain unconfirmed for now. “Zero” therefore functions both as the beginning of Dismantled’s new release cycle and as the return of material that has been evolving publicly for several years. The single is listed at 6:14 and will be available digitally in 24-bit/44.1 kHz resolution. Beatport currently categorises the track under Ambient / Experimental and lists it at 110 BPM, although Dismantled’s own history has always been rooted much more broadly in electro-industrial, EBM and electronic music. About Dismantled Dismantled began as a studio experiment by Gary Zon in late 2000, initially inspired by the sound of Front Line Assembly. Zon gradually added vocals and drew on influences from film, television and electronic music, developing a layered combination of electro-industrial electronics, melody and trance elements. A first demo appeared through mp3.com in 2001; Dependent Records subsequently included “Purity” on its Septic II compilation, and Metropolis Records contacted Zon later that year. The self-titled debut followed through Metropolis in 2002, with Post Nuclear arriving in 2004. Later releases included the Breed To Death EP, Standard Issue, The War Inside Me in 2011, the Whole Wide World EP in 2012 and The Hero in 2016. Metropolis currently lists “No Escape” from 2020 as Dismantled’s most recent release in its catalogue. “Zero” marks the project’s first new material in six years. For now, what is confirmed is simple: “Zero” arrives on 18 September via Metropolis Records, and a new Dismantled album follows in November. All available evidence points toward that album being the long-developed Endless, but complete official album details from Metropolis are still awaited.

items.body: British violist, singer and composer Sophie Sirota released the remix album “Pressure Drop Remixed” on 10 September 2026 through Coastal Electronauts, the Whitstable, Kent collective on which she is a co-organiser alongside Martin Glover‘s associate Peter Coyte. The ten-track set reworks Sirota’s 2025 debut “Pressure Drop” through contributions from Youth (Killing Joke bassist and producer Martin Glover, who supplies two remixes), 4hero, Coyte’s own Shape Navigator alias, 3Head/Al Mac, Will Materialise, smelliott, BorjeNotBorje, Grace Griffin Blustery Day and Riigs. The release-day single “If I Wrote A Song Would You Like It? (Shape Navigator Remix)” carries a new video edit by @diz_qo, the visual artist who works regularly with Coastal Electronauts. Of the clip, @diz_qo said: “I was seeking inspiration for it and found an old photo I’d taken years ago of what I believe to be some kind of radar equipment. It somehow resonated with the track – its sense of transmitting and receiving, of searching for a signal – and became the starting point for its visual language.” Two other tracks from the album preceded it as singles, each with its own @diz_qo video edit: Youth’s nine-minute rework of “50:50 Pure Trance”, which Side-Line covered on its own release, and “mood (4hero remix)”, whose video arrived the same month. Coyte mixed and mastered the original “Pressure Drop” album, which made his contribution to the remix set direct. Sirota commented: “Peter has given me considerable support and encouragement during my solo journey, and we have collaborated on several live projects. He also mixed and mastered the original ‘Pressure Drop’ album, so asking him to remix something from it was inevitable. The result is this beautiful track.” On the remix project as a whole, Sirota said she gave contributors free rein: “I’ve been fortunate to work with some incredible musicians during my career and it has been humbling to receive so many positive reactions to the idea of making it. What each contributor has sent back has resulted in a really eclectic variety of styles and sounds. I left each remix to their discretion and deliberately gave no direction or input.” She also pointed to newer names on the tracklist: “I’m particularly pleased to have had a number of younger artists provide unique interpretations of my tracks, including people I have met through the vibrant EMOM scene. After all, this is what gave me the initial encouragement and support to create the original album.” The full “Pressure Drop Remixed” tracklist runs: “50:50 Pure Trance – The Endless Carousel of Lust and Suffering Dub (Youth remix)”, “mood (4hero remix)”, “if i wrote a song would you like it? (Shape Navigator remix)”, “sophie’s tension (3Head/Al Mac remix)”, “i feel (Will Materialise remix)”, “holding te (smelliott remix)”, “i feel (BorjeNotBorje remix)”, “if i wrote a song would you like it? (Grace Griffin Blustery Day remix)”, “holding tension (Riigs remix)” and a second Youth reading, “50:50 Pure Ambient – The Savage Orient of the Heart Dub”. The album streams on Spotify, Apple Music and Amazon Music, and is available as a digital download on Bandcamp. Pressure Drop Remixed by Sophie Sirota About Sophie Sirota Sophie Sirota is a classically trained violist, singer and composer who began working as a session violist while at music college, going on to work as a session player, live performer, arranger and composer with Paul Weller, Kim Deal, Tindersticks, Beth Orton, Ed Harcourt, 4hero, D’Influence, Gabrielle and Robert Kirby; her Discogs profile lists close to 100 credits and a place in the Wrecking Crew Quartet. She has lived in Whitstable, Kent for more than two decades. In early 2023 she started performing solo material, built from electric viola, effects pedals and voice, at the monthly Coastal Electronauts electronic-music sessions in Whitstable, which she now helps organise. That work led to her debut album “Pressure Drop”, released on 24 October 2025 through Coastal Electronauts on digital, CD and a 100-copy vinyl edition, mixed and mastered by Peter Coyte. Record Collector called the album “a fine example of innovative artistic imagination”. “Pressure Drop Remixed”, out 10 September 2026, extends that debut into collaborative territory, opening Sirota’s viola-based material to Youth, 4hero, Coyte’s Shape Navigator project and a wider group of electronic producers. No dedicated Wikipedia page for Sirota could be found at the time of writing.

It is her first album for the label since 2023’s “All Above.” The lead single, “Let me know when you’re pure,” is out now on Bandcamp, Spotify and Apple Music, with the album available to pre-order on Bandcamp. “Temporary” was written after a period of personal grief and loss and
items.body: Berlin-based Dutch-Italian composer Aimée Portioli, who records as Grand River, returns to Editions Mego with her new album “Temporary”, out 20 November 2026. It is her first album for the label since 2023’s “All Above.” The lead single, “Let me know when you’re pure,” is out now on Bandcamp, Spotify and Apple Music, with the album available to pre-order on Bandcamp. “Temporary” was written after a period of personal grief and loss and centers on the interplay between resonant guitar work and electronics across eight tracks. The Bandcamp track listing runs: “18 circles to heaven,” “Come to stay,” “The crossing of the body, the crossing of the mind,” “The little we last,” “Let me know when you’re pure,” “From the other side,” “Maybe I am dead and this is paradise” and “Work of ending.” The eight titles form fragments of a longer sentence about transience, read in sequence across the record. Portioli commented on the album’s origins: “Sometimes, when travelling in places far from home that I know I will most likely never return to, or while accompanying someone I loved towards the end of their life, I become intensely aware of the singularity of the moment, and of how precious and sad this feels at the same time. It carries a particular weight because it will never happen again in quite the same way. Through experiences like these, I have gradually come to understand the temporary nature of all things. They taught me that to live is to experience the present while already feeling the trace of its disappearance, something both painful and blissful.” Temporary by Grand River Grand River live dates for ‘Temporary’ Portioli will premiere “Temporary” live at the Venice Music Biennale (Biennale Musica) before further European and Asian dates: 23 October 2026 – Biennale Musica, Venice, Italy (album premiere) 29 October 2026 – Berghain, Berlin, Germany 6 November 2026 – Mira Festival, Barcelona, Spain 7 November 2026 – Simple Things Festival, Bristol, UK 20 November 2026 – MUTEK, Tokyo, Japan Further dates have not been announced. About Grand River Grand River is the recording name of Aimée Portioli, a Dutch-Italian composer and sound designer based in Berlin. She began the project in 2014, after working as a sound engineer and composer for the Italian national radio station Radio 24 and co-founding the sound agency TapTempo studio with Luca Sammartin. Her first release, the EP “Crescente,” came out in 2017 on Spazio Disponibile, the label run by Donato Dozzy and Neel, and was named one of the year’s best EPs by XLR8R. Her debut album, “Pineapple,” followed in 2018, also on Spazio Disponibile. Portioli signed to the Vienna-based label Editions Mego for her second album, “Blink a Few Times to Clear Your Eyes,” released in September 2020. Since 2016 she has run the label One Instrument, which invites artists to record a piece using a single instrument; its catalog includes releases by Donato Dozzy and Felicity Mangan. Her third album, “All Above,” followed on Editions Mego in February 2023, dedicated to label founder Peter Rehberg, who died in 2021. In 2024 she released the collaborative album “In uno spazio immenso” with Abul Mogard on Caterina Barbieri’s label Light-Years. “Tuning the Wind,” a piece originally composed in 2022 for multichannel and 4DSOUND installations, was released as an album via Umor Rex in March 2025. Portioli has also contributed to compilations for Ghostly International and Tresor, and has performed at Berlin Atonal, CTM, MUTEK Montréal, Spain’s WOS festival, and venues including the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the Barbican in London and Berghain in Berlin. “Temporary,” out 20 November 2026 on Editions Mego, is her fourth solo studio album and the first live premiere of the record takes place at the Venice Music Biennale on 23 October 2026.

items.body: Italian electro-wave project TourdeForce releases a music video for “A Good Death”, a track from the band’s album “Leaving Nothing Left Behind,” released via My Owl Music on 27 February 2026. The video was filmed on location in Japan. “This video represents a watershed and introduces a new era,” TourdeForce’s Christian Ryder stated. The band plans to follow it within a month with a new single and video featuring lead singer Neviah Luneville on vocals. About TourdeForce TourdeForce is an Italian electro-wave and electro-pop project whose recent work Side-Line has followed closely. The band released the album “Vargtimmar” in December 2020, followed by two tribute singles to Death In June: “Six in the Key of Death” in January 2022 and a cover of “The Calling” with an accompanying video in March 2022, before revisiting older material on the compilation “Compendium vol. 1” that June. In April 2025, the project released a single paying tribute to the defunct EKP label. TourdeForce returned in February 2026 with the full-length album “Leaving Nothing Left Behind”, followed in March by an official video for the “LNLB” single mix. “A Good Death” is the latest video from that album, with a new single featuring vocalist Neviah Luneville expected next.

items.body: Margate, Kent-based musician Tim Horne has released “An Ocean Apart”, the first single from his new album “Transmutation”, out October 8, 2026, on Coastal Electronauts. Horne composes cinematic ambient and electronic music using synthesisers, acoustic instruments and field recordings. “An Ocean Apart” comes with a video by @diz_qo, built around artwork by Mariz Nigro, and the single is also available on Spotify and Apple Music. Horne describes “An Ocean Apart” as the emotional core of the album. “It forms the emotional core of the album and is imbued with paradoxical feelings of distance and closeness, isolation and connection. These are contradictory emotions I’ve oscillated between when looking back with unreliable memory and nostalgia,” he said. Tim Horne’s ‘Transmutation’ due October 8 “Transmutation” runs eight tracks: “Requiem,” “Halcyon,” “Biota,” “An Ocean Apart,” “Volta,” “Folie à Deux,” “Ascension” and “Metamorphosis.” Horne wrote, performed and produced every track himself, with additional mixing and mastering by Thomas Farmer and artwork by Mariz Nigro. The album was recorded towards the end of a long-term relationship and works through contradictory memories of joy and sorrow alongside an embrace of change. Horne layers flute and other acoustic instruments with analog, digital and modular synthesizers, often processing them until they no longer resemble their source material. He has pointed to Wendy Carlos, Kraftwerk, Boards of Canada, Sigur Rós, M83, Radiohead, Nils Frahm, Alessandro Cortini, R Beny, Emily Sprague, Ann Annie, Kaitlyn Aurelia Smith, Jogging House and Hainbach as influences on the record. Transmutation by Tim Horne “Transmutation” is available to pre-order now as a digital album and as a limited-edition CD in a card wallet, both through Bandcamp, with the full record following on release day. About Tim Horne Tim Horne is a musician based in Margate, Kent. He spent roughly a decade playing bass, synthesisers and backing vocals in bands including Linear Loveboxx, Inca Maps and Inigo Blue & The System before moving into solo work. He self-released two solo albums built from modular-synthesizer improvisation, “Rise” (2022) and “Clusters” (2023). Horne developed his current sound over two years through the regular live sessions hosted by Coastal Electronauts, a collective of electronic and experimental artists based in nearby Whitstable, and that process led to the eight tracks on “Transmutation.” The album, out October 8, 2026, on Coastal Electronauts, follows those two solo releases and is preceded by the single “An Ocean Apart.”

items.body: Dina Summer releases the synthpop single “Burning Heart” on 9 September 2026 via Iptamenos Discos. The track is part of the trio’s upcoming nine-track mini-album “Children Of The Night,” due 9 October 2026 on digital and vinyl. “Burning Heart” explores the pull of an imbalanced relationship, with the singer asking her partner to “cross the line” and return her affections. Sparkling organ synths sit against a propulsive dark bassline, pairing a nocturnal, club-ready sound with 1980s-style synthpop songwriting. Paris-based filmmaker Ceyda Yagiz directed the accompanying music video. “Children Of The Night” takes its title from Bela Lugosi’s line in the 1931 film “Dracula.” Iptamenos Discos will release the mini-album on black vinyl and on a blood red/black marbled vinyl edition, alongside the digital format. Dina Summer will tour behind the record, with festival dates including Wave Gotik Treffen, Amphi Festival, E-Tropolis Festival, Grauzone Festival, Out Of Line Weekender, Katzenclub Festival, Extramuralhas and Baroeg, plus headline shows in Berlin, London, Paris, Athens, Bogotá, São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Santiago and Buenos Aires. About Dina Summer Dina Summer is the Berlin-based collaborative project of Greek-German dark-disco duo Local Suicide and Bavarian electronic producer Kalipo, who began working together in 2019. The project draws on 1980s Italo disco, new wave, EBM and early-2000s electroclash for a dark, retro-futuristic synthpop sound. Dina Summer released the single “Schall & Rauch” in October 2024, then announced the mini-album “Children Of The Night” in June 2026. The trio followed with the singles “Bats in Paris” in July and “Rat Race” in August, and now “Burning Heart” arrives ahead of the mini-album’s 9 October release on Iptamenos Discos.

items.body: In 1998, a remarkable album was released as a collaborative exchange between Sonar and Muslimgauze. Eric van Wonterghem and Dirk Ivens (Sonar) created four remixes of tracks by Bryn Jones (Muslimgauze), and the process was reciprocated. However, what wasn’t known at the time was that Bryn Jones had actually produced a total of 16 remixes, leaving it up to Eric and Dirk to decide what to do with them. Following the release, performances featuring both projects were even planned, but tragedy struck when Bryn Jones passed away in early 1999. The British project Muslimgauze was extraordinary—a project I deeply admired for its sound and its unique blend of Tribal and Middle Eastern influences. Now, so many years later, these Belgian legends have decided to release the original remixes Muslimgauze created for Sonar as a standalone album, undoubtedly driven by deep respect and admiration for Bryn Jones’s masterful body of work. The result is surprising, presenting a completely transformed Sonar sound that fits seamlessly into the Muslimgauze universe. The Belgians’ signature Power-Noise is absorbed by the force of Tribal rhythms and an Eastern atmosphere, characterized by the authentic sounds of traditional instruments. Layered on top are samples of plaintive chants and voices that further enhance the mood. Muslimgauze didn’t merely create remixes; Jones undertook a complete reconstruction of the Sonar material. The overall sound is highly minimalist and perfectly embodies the Muslimgauze aesthetic. I am also struck by the brilliant stereo effects emanating from the speakers, which lend an extra touch of distinction to the production. Through this album, Muslimgauze sounds as if the project is still alive—or perhaps newly reborn. As far as I’m concerned, this is a wonderful experience. (Rating:8). Listen to “Outtake 3”: Outtake 3 by Sonar vs Muslimgauze About Sonar Sonar is the Belgian industrial and techno side-project of Dirk Ivens, also known for his work in Klinik and Dive. The project began with Ivens working alongside Patrick Stevens (Hypnoskull); Eric Van Wonterghem (Insekt, Monolith) later joined as the group’s other core member. Sonar released its self-titled debut album in 1996, followed by “Dislocated” and “On Mission Inside” in 1997. In 1998, Sonar exchanged remixes with British artist Muslimgauze (Bryn Jones, 17 June 1961 – 14 January 1999) for the collaborative album “Sonar vs Muslimgauze”, released via Prodam Records. Jones died in January 1999, shortly after the exchange was completed. “Outtakes” gathers the remaining Muslimgauze-made remixes of Sonar material that were left unused at the time.

items.body: Made your hell from the fire inside Played in flames that burned you alive What went through your head when you lost your mind The true tragedy is the world decides Something ancient in the crowd gathers around a famous death. A murder becomes spectacle; strangers study photographs, motives, wounds, and final moments as though proximity to horror might grant some secret knowledge. The macabre is easiest to enjoy when the dead are unknown to us, when grief belongs to another household and blood has no familiar name. Tragedy, then, can be consumed as theater, mystery, even entertainment. We call it curiosity, but often it is appetite dressed in respectable clothes. Civilization may depend, in part, on remembering that every spectacle was first a human life actually lived. We’ve seen it played out countless times in real life, as well as in profound films like Day of the Locust. Seattle goth dance-punk trio Holy Death Temple return with their fourth single, Nobody Loved You, a murder ballad that is shamelessly poppy and driven by a fiery bassline and fierce drumming that make the song feel almost indecently buoyant. Bryan Edward’s programming gives the track the clean immediacy of gothic synth-pop, while Jon Barrysmith’s drums keep the floor moving beneath it. Wren Rose folds guitar, synth, and backing vocals into the arrangement without crowding the hook. Edward handles lead vocals, guitar, and programming; Barrysmith (Year of the Cobra, Rifflord) takes drums; Rose (Broken Focus) supplies guitar, synth, and backing vocals. There is a little Sisters of Mercy gloom in the DNA, some Depeche Mode pop precision, and enough dance-punk velocity to place Holy Death Temple comfortably alongside ACTORS, Sextile, and VR SEX. Nobody Loved You finds its real character in the gap between what the body hears and what the lyrics are saying. The song examines the public appetite that gathers around violent death, particularly the urge to turn murder into a referendum on character. Someone dies, and almost immediately spectators begin sorting themselves into camps, prosecuting the dead, defending the killer, reconstructing motives, and deciding who deserved what. Condemnation becomes a recreational drug with excellent engagement numbers. The man at the center of the lyrics is controlling, cruel, hungry for power, and shaped by abandonment that eventually curdles into brutality. His wife endures pain and sacrifice until the arrangement ends with death. Holy Death Temple lets the listener enjoy condemning him for a while, then complicates that satisfaction by asking why everyone becomes so obsessed with determining whether a death was justified while showing far less interest in how a human being arrived at such a miserable destination. That question feels particularly sharp in an age where high-profile killings become participatory entertainment, complete with amateur detectives, moral tribunals, leaked photographs, podcast episodes, TikTok theories, and millions of strangers inspecting somebody else’s catastrophe from bed. Bryan Edward seems fully aware of how strange it is to package all of this inside something so catchy: “Never thought we’d explore our fascination with high-profile murders and repressed Erasure influence in the same song, but here we are,” he quips. “…Nobody Loved You is a mercy-killed synth-pop demo resurrected with a hook intended for a completely different track. Our best moments come from botched experiments and happy accidents.” Listen to Nobody Loved You below and order the single here. Nobody Loved You by Holy Death Temple Nobody Loved You is a bright synth-pop ‘mistake’ with a body in the trunk, built for the dance floor while staring straight at one of civilization’s uglier appetites: the thrill of death when the grief belongs to somebody else. Follow Holy Death Temple: Instagram YouTube The post Seattle’s Holy Death Temple Returns With Gothic Synthpop Murder Ballad “Nobody Loved You” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Hands in the sky and then we die Our hearts have joined the thousand We take a step into the night Opening our eyes brings a new dawn The Goth subculture has survived for nearly half a century partly because every few years somebody remembers that death can be absurd. Strip away that humour and the genre starts resembling a homeowners’ association for people with excellent boots: approved haircuts, approved records, approved photographs taken beside approved statues in approved cemeteries. Then Comes Silence have enough mileage behind them to recognize the danger. Remaker Redeemer finds the Stockholm trio Alex Svenson, Jonas Fransson, and Hugo Zombie treating the graveyard as a playground again. Then Comes Silence fortunately remembers that a black shirt is still a shirt. The album itself is conceived as a diptych, with “Requiem” representing darkness and “Ballroom” representing light. “Everything exists in contrast,” the band says. Remaker Redeemer introduces the “Ballroom” half of the band’s forthcoming Requiem Ballroom, due November 20. The band explains that the song “is about new life, being reborn with old sins washed away. A kind of cleansing, a fresh start, and the feeling of beginning again. The choice of instruments and sounds on this track was also a way to explore something a bit different this time.” Svenson’s bass plants every movement firmly beneath the feet, while Fransson’s drums drive the song with a dark, danceable force reminiscent of Killing Joke’s Night Time era. Svenson’s grave, commanding vocals strengthen the comparison, while Zombie’s guitar cuts through with a bright, sharp edge. There is genuine pleasure in the performance, closer to liberation than solemn contemplation, which suits a song concerned with starting over. Rebirth here apparently requires amplification, eyeliner, and several people dressed as failed medical experiments. The song’s lyrics treat death as a passage toward renewal, moving from surrender and darkness toward another existence. Closed eyes, raised hands, joined hearts, and the arrival of dawn suggest a collective transformation, while the repeated call to a remaker and redeemer turns rebirth into an act of cleansing: old sins washed away, one life surrendered, and another beginning on the other side. The video makes the album’s concept pleasantly mischievous. Renewal takes place among monsters. Cleansing occurs in a room full of freaks. Life returns while death watches from the front row. Directed by Damon Zurawski of Future Legends Films, the video places the band before a congregation of ghouls, Droogs, demons, grotesques, and evil babies. Yes, evil babies that look like escapees from the bargain bin of some forbidden 1970s horror shop, which immediately gives the clip more personality than another five minutes of serious men staring into industrial fog. Zurawski photographs the performance beautifully while allowing the absurdity to breathe. Svenson holds court on bass and vocals with severe composure while Fransson hammers away behind him and Zombie sends guitar across the room in sharp strokes. Around them, the assembled creatures stare, convulse, leer, and generally behave like the clientele of a nightclub whose liquor license was issued by Satan. Watch the video for Remaker Redeemer below: Rock music periodically develops the delusion that dignity equals importance, an especially fatal mistake for any subculture born from makeup, theatrical clothing, cheap smoke machines, horror films, and teenagers trying to scandalize their parents. The original punk impulse understood spectacle as provocation. Somewhere along the road, certain corners of underground culture began treating their uniforms with the solemnity of military dress. That final joke may be the best one. Subcultures survive through mutation, bad taste, risk, exaggeration, and people willing to make fools of themselves in public. Then Comes Silence understands that preservation without mischief eventually becomes embalming. Remaker Redeemer puts the corpse back on its feet, gives it a bass guitar, and lets the evil babies dance. Then Comes Silence are currently on tour in mainland Europe. items.body: Punk may have changed the musical landscape and proved that anyone with a guitar and a mission statement could start a band, but the years that followed expanded punk’s simplicity in countless exciting directions. Sometimes, it blows my mind just how many incredible bands and movements formed in the wake of the punk explosion. From 1976-1982 alone, the sheer amount of musical creativity is staggering, with so many bands quick to combine punk’s feral, DIY essence with art rock instrumentation; spacier, dubbed-out rhythms; bleak industrial textures; and much, much more. In the UK, hundreds of bands formed in the wake of the Sex Pistols, who begat Joy Division, The Banshees, and Cabaret Voltaire, who begat thousands of other bands that we all know and love today. One of the most lasting and beloved bands from the original UK post-punk boom was Sad Lovers & Giants. Formed in Watford in 1980 by Garce (Simon) Allard, guitarist Simon Blanchard, bassist Cliff Silver, drummer Nigel Pollard, and keyboardist/saxophonist David Wood, Sad Lovers & Giants (SLAG for short), quickly signed with Last Movement and Midnight Music and released a string of crucial early singles as a statement of intent. During those early years, the band was extremely prolific, cutting two moody full-length LPs in addition to these singles, each track as powerful as the last. The band caught the ear of John Peel and cultivated a devout cult following both on the strength of their studio recordings as well as their explosive live show. Soon after, the band would splinter, with Blanchard and Powell leaving to form The Snake Corps. In 1987, SLAG would reform with a new lineup and release three incredible records that saw the band expanding their sound and influencing the budding dream pop movement. 1987’s The Mirror Test is a landmark album for me personally, and it’s impressive to hear the album’s lush textures reflected in countless bands today. Again, in 1991, the band went on hiatus, but have since returned in the new millennium and have rekindled the spark that brought them together all those years ago. Since reuniting in 2002 (and again in 2009 with Pollard), the band has performed hundreds of gigs (including their first series of shows in North America in 2016), recorded a session for LA’s Part Time Punks, released a handful of standalone singles, and recorded two full-length LPs. Their latest release, this year’s The Weight of Forgotten Dreams, features ten new tracks, all of which stay true to SLAG’s majestic sound and atmospheric energy. The album is currently available on CD, digital, and vinyl, and will be followed up by a highly anticipated documentary that aims to capture the band’s many evolutions and highlights over their 40+ year career. We had the chance to catch up with the current incarnation of SLAG, including vocalist/guitarist Garce Allard, original drummer Nigel Pollard, and current members Tony McGuinness, Will Hicks, and Ian Gibson, about the new album, the band’s legacy, and more. Former guitarist and close friend Simon Blanchard also drops in for a spell… Congratulations on the new album! Can you tell us a bit about the recording of it? Garce: Our writing and recording processes aren’t separate. We have home studios in which we produce demos that are saved into a SLAG Dropbox, there are files for demos, instrumentals and raw vocal and sax stems. If anyone comes up with a demo it goes in the appropriate file. I always save a AIFF of my raw vocals at every stage. Usually what happens next is that the demos are played at rehearsal and everybody contributes ideas. Quite often these ideas are road tested at live shows and subtle changes are made, then it’s back to the original demo which gets an upgrade. When the demo file and instrumental file look like they are full enough to consider an album we produce a provisional running order and work out what needs doing to each track before it can be handed over to Igor and Tony to mix. Effectively, all the recording is done at home. The only time we go into a recording studio is if I need to ‘perform’ my vocals as we often notice they are different when I sing them in front of other people. This didn’t happen with the new record, so every vocal was recorded in the studio at the bottom of my garden. On a personal note, I write all the lyrics and whilst the others freely critique them I mainly use Nigel as a specific sounding board while a song develops, but Tony ultimately produces my vocals from the raw stems that I have comp’d and uploaded to the Dropbox file. Tony is the only person on the planet I would trust to edit the actual words I write as happened with a song on The Weight of Forgotten Dreams where I just got lost in thickets of words which needed a sympathetic pruning! Very occasionally we look in the demo files and there’s a long forgotten piece of music that is 95% album ready. This actually happened on this record. It’s been eight years between Mission Creep and The Weight Of Forgotten Dreams – were you working on the record all this time, or were you focused on other things? Garce: Song writing is a perpetual thing but the other project we’ve worked on over the last three years is the SLAG documentary being produced by Jean Paul Van Mierlo who did the excellent Adrian Borland film Walking in the Opposite Direction. This is with the same film maker Marc Waltman. This is your second record working with Igor Garanin – can you share some stories about working together? Garce: Igor is a mix engineer Tony knows through Above & Beyond and he did such a great job on Mission Creep that we used him again on the new album. Tony works with Igor in the studio and then sends us mixes for comment. How has your songwriting style evolved over the years? Garce: If you mean the way we get to a finished album, then the human process is very similar but the technology available now means we don’t have to do the traditional ‘recording studio’ thing. In that sense, we are effectively self-producing, whereas before, the person paying for the studio, i.e., Nick Ralph if it was Midnight Music, had a large say in the overall production decisions and the ‘style’ of the finished songs. But I think what you mean is the evolution of our style of song. Many other people will have many differing views on this and which album they like best and I accept it has changed subtly from album to album. Not a lot has changed vocally other than I’ve got better at writing melodies and perhaps more focused on saying what I want, in the way I want, in order to compliment the music and bring out the best in a song. Changes in personnel obviously bring an element of change so the key personnel swap was Tony McGuinness for Simon Blanchard on guitar after the second album. I could write an essay on that. Then there was Juliet Sainsbury (currently lives in LA) on keyboards in the eighties, she was the most accomplished keyboardist we’ve had so what she plays the others wouldn’t have been able to. Then we’ve had Cliff Silver on bass replaced by Ian Gibson and both are like chalk and cheese as musicians and songwriters. The net result of all this in my opinion, is that if anything the cinematic quality of the ambient strings and ‘wet’ noise has become more lush and expansive but…to a listener coming to the band now, the songs on the latest album have all the same sonic qualities and idiosyncrasies as all the other albums. We have a distinctive SLAG sound which we understand and respect. Nigel: Our style has not really changed over the years; we all know what makes a good SLAG song . Our songs stand the test of time, and I personally cannot distinguish between songs written 40 years ago to those that are on our latest album. Garce has and continues to write very emotional and evocative lyrics which many fans can connect with. Can you expand on some of the lyrics or themes behind the record? Garce: “We will be ashes, we will be silent and old, we will be wisdom, we will be left in the cold” were the lyrics I wrote as a twenty four year old for our second single “Things We Never Did.” I am now far older than the age I envisaged in that song and I have no intention of being silent or of being left in the cold! Broadly, I would describe my lyrics as ‘English Melancholia’ but I noticed a wry-ness creeping in over the course of this recent album, although given that I am writing about the state of the world as I currently see it there’s precious little to chuckle about; call it gallows humour. As a device, I often write against a fictional dystopian backdrop (“Asylum Town,” “Repentance Day,” “Down To The Wire”), but increasingly the dystopia has become reality since the last album in 2018. Unfortunately, that does seem to be the case, doesn’t it? Sad to think that all the prophecies, whether it be in lyrics or films or literature has come true, in a sense. On a lighter, but related note, what else, other than music, do you tend to draw inspiration from? Garce: Literature and Art Nigel: Differing cultures and the great outdoors. Sad Lovers & Giants have always had such iconic artwork across both your singles and LPs. The covers alone really convey such a strong sense of emotion and perfectly reflect the music in my opinion. I’d love to hear more about what inspires your album artwork. Garce: Simon Blanchard designed the sleeves for the first three singles, including the image for “Lost In a Moment” (girl in armchair with teddy bear!), which is one that is particularly well known. Given that he also wrote much of the songs I think his design choices were intuitively in alignment with his songwriting. Midnight Music did the design work for many subsequent releases but they were building on the foundations he had laid. We asked Simon to design The Weight of Forgotten Dreams as he did such a great job with the previous album, Mission Creep and Cherry Red Records asked him to design the box set they released. Simon: Well it’s imortant to remember I can’t claim credit for all the band’s sleevework and Tony’s contribution is not to be underestimated. It’s not always easy to provide a visual foil for their music, but having been there since the beginning, I probably have a basic understanding of the strange world they inhabit. There’s usually a lot of trial and error and this time it was helpful to have access to some of Garce’s original paintings, which I montaged-up with the photography. To me it felt that the result sat well with the music and luckily the band liked it. Will you be touring for this record? Garce: In SLAG world there are three things happening currently. The Weight Of Forgotten Dreams, the film and then the live double album recorded for the film, so we will be playing live more over the next two years to coincide with this creative phase. I was happy to hear that the band finally came to the US after all these years, but sadly I live in New York and couldn’t make it to the West Coast/Austin shows. Do you plan to come back to North America at all? Garce: We want to come back and at some point over this next two years would be great timing but we are not in any specific discussions at present. Obviously as we did the West Coast plus Canada and SXSW in Austin last time, the East Coast and New York would be a priority next time. In the Breeze-era lineup. Photo by Cliff Ash. Looking back to the formation of the band, can you tell us a bit about how you all came together? Garce: The band was originally formed by Simon, Nigel and Dave Wood, who were at school together. They were called The Traumatics and they recruited an outside bass player called Steve Carter who sadly died quite recently. Dave played tenor sax and both Simon and Steve sang. At that time I was playing guitar (and singing backing vocals) in another local band called Suspect Device and we knew each other from playing together supporting a well known local band called Mr E and The Imaginations. Mr E had supported The Ruts at The Marquee club and the guitarist and singer of The Ruts were at our gig. I knew Dave Wood from drinking and playing pool together at The Feathers in Rickmansworth and he invited me to audition as the singer of The Traumatics. From that first meeting we knew it would work because we shared the same musical tastes. Our first London gigs were performed as The Traumatics with Steve Carter on bass. When we did “50:50” he sang it and I played keyboards. We changed the name from The Traumatics to Sad Lovers & Giants in January 1981. Sometime after the first single we brought in Cliff Silver on bass who we knew from playing with other Watford bands that he was in. We also bought a string synth and Simon began experimenting with spacial guitar sounds. Dave began playing the string synth more than the sax. Simon: We formed pretty soon after the punk explosion in the late seventies. We had been listening to rock music for years before that as young teenagers but it suddenly became very clear that you could be in a band with only very rudimentary music skills. We slowly got better – but not that much. The Traumatics. Photo credit unknown. Mid-80s lineup. Photo by Nick Ralph. Was there a coherent scene in Watford? Garce: There were a lot of young bands who all knew each other and played and drank in the same pubs. There was the Watford Pub Rock competition run by the owner of the local music shop and there were several fanzines. Apart from ‘our sort of music’ i.e. Post Punk/New Wave/Alternative/Art School bands, there were other more mainstream rock and blues bands mainly comprised of older musicians. Watford was a seething mass of music and musicians but probably no different to many large towns in the early eighties. The UK music scene at that time was quite remarkable looking back on it. I listened to a BBC radio 4 programme the other day whose basic premise was that the counterculture of the ’60s didn’t die out but was boosted by punk and morphed into the indie scene of the ’80s. But then the establishment pushed back, Thatcherism (Margaret Thatcher, prime minister 1979 to 1990) was in effect a counter-counterculture where alternative views were discouraged. On the whole we weren’t overtly political but if you were in one of those young bands then you knew who the enemy was and just doing it was resistance of sorts. That was the true source of the apparent coherence. A disparate collection of bands from Watford and nearby towns got together and put out an album called The Thing From The Crypt but the DIY record scene was just a reflex in the instinctive resistance to the establishment. I love that compilation and was very happy to pick up the Dark Entries reissue a few years back! Otherwise, the band has such an iconic catalog of tracks, including bangers like “50:50,” “Seven Kinds of Sin,” “In Flux,” “Colourless Dream,” etc. that are still heard in clubs today. How do you feel about the band’s legacy thus far? Garce: When we started we were defining our sound and every new song we wrote was a step into the unknown. When we reformed in 2009 we were coming off the back of a reputation built over thirty years and eight albums so from then on there was a pressure to maintain the standards we had set. As a live band we’ve surpassed those early standards which comes not only from experience but from having a huge back catalogue of great songs to choose from; we have the songs and we know how to use them. These days we’ve scaled our live show up for some seriously large gigs and have sold out 1200 capacity venues in our own name but we are still a cult band albeit with a huge worldwide following. Sometimes I dream about suddenly becoming a mainstream act but in reality I’m quite happy being where we are. Which begs the question, “if it’s not about world domination what is it about?” Answer: the music, the fans, the international travel, the ‘pinch yourself’ moments when we achieve something surprising like having “Colourless Dream” used in the Netflix Andy Warhol series. But above all it’s about the shared experience of doing it all with your mates and…still being able to make music. As a post punk-eighties band, we are always going to be remembered for those first two albums but there are eight others and Spotify has helped get them heard with around 150,000 plays a month. I’m very proud of all of them; they are all unique and have their own story to tell. The trick with the last two has been to keep our essential ‘sound’ whilst conforming to modern production expectations because fans listen to the work recorded in the analogue world of the early eighties and the production standards of that era were completely different, nevertheless they are synonymous with what the fans think of as SLAG. That is acceptable when it’s tinged with nostalgia but not in the modern world. If I remember correctly there was hardly any compression used on the early albums, can you believe that? So I think The Weight of Forgotten Dreams sits well in the legacy scheme of things. But what next? Do we write one last happy album? Hopefully there will be many more to come! Can you share some personal highlights from over the years? Garce: Showcasing at SXSW in 2016 Nigel: Playing our first gig as Sad Lovers & Giants in our hometown of Rickmansworth, recording our second single (“Colourless Dream”) in Surrey Sound where Siouxsie and the Banshees had been recording their LP Juju. More recently playing to 5,000 people at the 2024 Visor fest in Murcia, Spain, with the Sun going down – Magical! Tony: Highlight for me was selling out Echoplex in LA at the end of our first US tour. Ian: I enjoy playing live so my personal highlights are: The first time we played The Marquee in Wardour Street – I felt it was a proper rock venue that I’d previously been to as a punter, it felt a bit surreal to me to be up on that stage in front of paying punters. Another surreal moment was my overseas debut at Club Isla near Valencia, which felt like an enormous gig to me. The Echoplex in LA was special. The festival in Murcia was too….so many great gigs. SLAG at the Echoplex in 2016. Photo by Terry Howick. Will: Playing live is definitely my favourite part of being in Sad Lovers & Giants. I love meeting the fans and other bands that we play with, I love seeing places around the world from a perspective that I wouldn’t be able to access without the network of promoters and friends that the band cultivates. I love feeling the connection with our audience during a performance – which feels like a celebration of the band, every time, and I feel privileged to be part of it and to help contribute to the legacy. In particular, I will always remember our US tour – which was a huge undertaking for the band – a chaotic yet rewarding experience of massive drives, downtown motels and passionate crowds. What’s next for the band? Garce: We play two gigs in Italy this October, then we put the final touches to the film for the rest of this year. The live album will be pressed and ready for release around then but the exact timing of everything depends on the film. Then we have a gig on a boat in Paris in March followed hopefully by a small tour of Portugal and Spain. After that there will inevitably be a series of gigs in all the usual places, namely Holland, Germany and Greece. Meanwhile the demo file will begin filling up again! § Sad Lovers & Giants’ new album The Weight of Forgotten Dreams is out now! Listen via Spotify and order here. Follow Sad Lovers & Giants Linktree Website Instagram Facebook Spotify Documentary Kickstarter Header photo by Simon Blanchard The post Down To The Wire — An Interview With Sad Lovers & Giants appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: If you ask me (and you are, since you're reading this review), the power of Green Lung always lay in the tension between their rock n' roll groove and their power ballad delivery. For me, neither part was strong enough to stand on its own; rather, the way each set up the other was what made Green Lung so good. Moving from "Hunters in the Sky" into "Oceans of Time" for example (both from This Heathen Land) just gets me every time. The former is ripping and roaring track arranged around a monstrously infectious chorus while the latter is a gothic, bombastic, and flamboyant tribute to one of the best divas to ever do it, Count Vlad Dracula himself. It's the tension and the payoff that keeps me coming back again and again to the album and, indeed, to Green Lung's entire backlog.Maybe you disagree; maybe you love Green Lung simply for their ability to conjure the spirit of rock n' roll at their tip of their guitars and infuse it with just enough stoner metal magic. I know at least one person like this and while I disagree, I respect the position; there is no doubt that Green Lung rock. If that's what you're after, then Necropolitan, their upcoming release, has it in spades. From the big main riff of "Black Magic Radio" to the soaring solo and vocals of "Together in Death" (some of the best from the band on both accounts), Necropolitan is all rock. There's a touch of the power ballad on tracks like "To the Gallows Born", which closes the album, and even some at the beginning of the aforementioned "Together in Death". But that's about it; the rest is dedicated to the worship of the riff.And, for me, this is also where the album's weakness lies. I found myself getting a bit lost in the sea of licks, grooves, and ear-worm targeted choruses. When I tuned in, everything I heard was good, even very good. But it was hard to tune in, as the mode of the album maintained the same pace, the same vibe, and the same intent. I longed for the contrast; the first two tracks went by and I headbanged and danced and had fun but then I wanted to be a bit wistful, you know? To raise my arms in praise of a higher power. To dream of the trees. Green Lung stuff, you know? And it was completely absent. There are so many examples from Green Lung's career that I could add to the ones in the first paragraph - "May Queen", "One For Sorrow", "Graveyard Sun". These are some of Green Lung's best and most memorable tracks, exactly because they temper the hot, sharp steel of Green Lung's groove with a colder, more epic, and more grandiose iron that, in my opinion, is sorely needed. However, as I said, what's on this album is very good - no one will catch me skipping a Green Lung track when the window is down and the car is going fast and I want to rock the fuck out. But sometimes I want other things and Green Lung's previous albums gave that to me. Necropolitan does not. Alas! Necropolitan by GREEN LUNG

items.body: 2026.09.10 2026年11月15日までソウルで上演中 いまミュージカル・ファンから熱い視線が注がれている「韓国ミュージカル」（韓国で上演されているミュージカル）。現在ソウルでは、日本でも大人気の演目『エリザベート』（脚本・作詞：ミヒャエル・クンツェ、作曲：シルヴェスター・リーヴァイ）が上演されている。ここでは、実際に現地へ観劇しに行った編集部員（ミュージカル愛好家のアラサー）が、チケットの取りかたから、会場へのアクセス、劇場での楽しみかたなどを紹介する。 掛川桃花 「音楽の友」編集者 神奈川県相模原市出身。音高、音大ピアノ科を経て、現在「音楽の友」編集者。©ヒダキトモコ 詳しく見る 電車で行ける！劇場までのアクセス方法 昨年から映画館で上映されているシリーズ「韓国ミュージカル on screen」をきっかけに、日本のミュージカル・ファンに広く知られ、大注目となっているのが「韓国ミュージカル（韓ミュ）」。ソウルでは8月から大人気の演目『エリザベート』（韓国エリザ）が、EMKカンパニーによって上演されている。 まず「韓国でミュージカルを観る」と聞いて、お隣の国と言っても海外だし、初心者でも大丈夫かしら…… と一瞬でも思われたかたのために、まずは日本から会場までのアクセスをご紹介。 東京から仁川空港まで早くて2時間、空港からソウル駅までの直通の電車で約1時間（別料金で特急もある）。ソウル駅から『エリザベート』の会場となる「ブルースクエア ウリ銀行ホール」までは電車で約20〜30分で到着する。ソウル駅からは途中で1回乗り換えはあるが、路線がすべて数字（4番線→6番線）で示されているのでわかりやすい。ちなみに最寄りの「漢江鎮（ハンガンジン）駅」は大ヒット韓国ドラマ『梨泰院（イテウォン）クラス』の舞台である梨泰院駅の隣の駅と考えると覚えやすい。劇場は駅から直結なので、迷わず到着することができた。 ソウル駅では4番線に乗り、サムガクチ駅で6番線に乗り換える。ちなみに韓国ではGoogleマップがあまり使えないため（私の場合はなぜかGmailの送信もできなかった）、地図アプリ「NAVER Maps」の使用をおすすめする 劇場「ブルースクエア」は最寄り駅から直結！ 劇場の外から 観劇前には隣の駅の梨泰院（イテウォン）に立ち寄り。カッコイイ兄貴たちが歩いてきそう（笑） 梨泰院にあるコーヒーショップ「coffee of course」で、観劇への高まる気持ちをコーヒーで抑える 日本からの道のりを示すと少々長く感じるが、ソウルを拠点にした旅行と考えれば、とっても気軽。もちろん、日本を朝に出発すれば夕方には観劇が可能だ。 私が観劇したのは夜の公演（19時30分開演、終演は22時くらい）だったが、この時間帯でも治安はよく、タクシーなどを使わなくても、日本と同じようにホテルまで電車で帰れる。想像以上に好アクセスで、韓国旅行が初めてでも挑戦しやすい！と感じたことをまずはお伝えしたい。 夜公演を前に韓国現地で購入したイヤリング（約800円）。観劇のお供として（おみやげも兼ねて）エリザベートの有名な肖像画にある髪飾りに近いデザインを探しました アクセサリーショップ「NYUNYU（ニューニュー）」明洞店は、手ごろな価格帯で、とにかく品揃えが豊富 日本語対応ありのアプリでチケット購入 現地入りのハードルが下がったところで、私が行ったチケットの取りかたを紹介する。 チケット予約＆購入は、サイト「NOL World 」内で行った。ほかにも「メロンチケット」などがある。 購入時までに必要な事前準備としては、まずはアプリのインストール、パスポートや顔認証などをふくめた会員登録をしておくこと。日本語対応があり、パスポートの読み取りもスムーズで、デジタルの最先端を感じる。クレジットカードの登録は、購入時のタイミングでOK。 発売日になったら、アプリを開き、演目を選べば購入画面に進むことができる。……という仕組みなのだが、私が購入した際は販売初日だからか、アプリからの購入ができず、ブラウザからサイトにログインして購入した。 そもそも日本だと、アクセス集中のため購入サイトにつながらない、という現象が多々起こるが、このアプリの場合は「現在●人待ちです」と表示されるので、開いたままで待つことができて、鬼のような顔をして何度もページを開き直す必要がなくて便利。残席には余裕ありで、当日券を買うことも可能だった。 ちなみに、日本ではミュージカルは半年前くらいからチケットが販売されるが、今回の韓国ミュージカル『エリザベート』は初日の約1ヶ月前からの販売。上演日時の詳細が発表されたのも約1ヶ月半前だった。そのため上演期間だけ押さえておいて、航空券とホテルだけ先に予約しておいた。 チケットは、日本と同様に座席にランクがあり、最も良い席で約18000円、安い席で約9000円程度。 サイト「NOL World」の『エリザベート』チケット購入画面 サイト「NOL World」 予習にもおすすめの「EMKミュージカル」の公式YouTube。今回エリザベートを演じるキャストたちそれぞれの《私だけに》（エリザベートが歌う名ナンバー）などを聴ける 開演1時間前の到着がおすすめ さあ、いよいよ現地での観劇。建物に入ってすぐ、劇場の入り口扉があるのが少々驚き。各階、各扉の前にスタッフがいて、そこでチケットを見せて入るシステムだ。 ここで思わぬ落とし穴が。到着したら、チケット発券機で紙チケットを発券するのだが、このホールの仕組み上、劇場の扉を出ればそこは公の場。トイレ休憩の際にチケットを座席に置いてきてしまうと再入場できなくなる。案の定チケットを忘れた私は入り口で引き留められ、スタッフのかたに座席まで着いてきてもらった。本当にすみませんでした。 ミュージカルはもちろん韓国語での上演だが、海外からの観光客にも優しい、AI機能がついた字幕眼鏡を借りることができる。会場にレンタルスペースがあり、そこで紙に必要事項を記入、料金（日本円で1500円くらい）を支払い、パスポートを預ける。「え？パスポートを預けるの！？」と不安に思われるかたもいると思うが、きちんとスタッフが管理しているのがわかり、安心して預けられた。終演後、字幕眼鏡を返すタイミングで引き取る。 この字幕眼鏡、はじめのうちは多少の違和感があったのだか、結果的に借りてとてもよかった！必要に応じて付けたり外したりして活用。多少、場面と字幕のズレが生じることもあったが、ほぼ問題ない。日本でも劇団四季などが導入しているようだ。初期設定に少々時間がかかるので、余裕を持って座席でスタンバイしたい。 会場には、キャスト表やポスター以外に、フォトスポットや、有料のフォトブース、関連グルメや、グッズ売り場などなど、『エリザベート』の世界観を味わうコーナーがたくさん用意されている。余裕を持って40分前くらいに到着したが、かなり時間が足りずに焦った。おすすめは開演1時間前の到着。 大きく張り出されている当日のキャスト表 無料のフォトスポット （左）字幕眼鏡をレンタルするカウンター、（右）チケットを発券する機械 初体験の字幕眼鏡！ 観劇の記念に撮るのが楽しい！ 韓国ミュージカル『エリザベート』オリジナル・デザインのプリクラ（？）。シール状ではなく、写真の形で印刷されて出てくる（約1000円） 撮影はスピーディに進むため、あらかじめポージングを用意しておくのがオススメ。最後にQRが表示されて、そこから撮影時の動画&写真データも送ってもらえるので、スマホをすぐに取り出せるようにしておくと安心 エリザベートなりきりフォト・ブース。こちらもプリクラ機のような感じ トートなりきりフォトブース。こちらを体験してみたが、スタジオで撮影したかのようなクオリティの高い仕上がりにびっくり！（約1200円） 会場では『エリザベート』をテーマにしたオリジナルのフードも販売されている。これらを飲まなかった&食べなかったのを、あとから後悔…… おみやげに購入したグッズたち。歌&ピアノ伴奏の楽譜（約1600円）と扇子（約1000円） 「韓国エリザ」ならではの世界観、迫力の歌声 オペラなどと同様、プロダクションごとに演出に違いがあるミュージカル。日本で観劇した東宝版とはまた違う、ストーリーの浮かび上がらせ方がおもしろかった。「韓国ミュージカル on screen 」は俳優に寄ったカットが多いため（これはこれで大変良き）、舞台で全体を俯瞰してみると、映像では気づかなかった部分もたくさんあった。 またキャストたちの迫力ある生歌には痺れた。とくにトート役のソ・ギョンス氏の歌は、エレガントさも感じられる芯の通った歌声。天井突き抜けるようなパワーあふれる《最後のダンス》を浴びられるのは劇場ならではの経験。現地に来てよかったー（嬉し泣き）と心から感じるリアル観劇だった。 時代と国境を超え、いまでも愛され続ける皇妃エリザベート。 現地観劇は直近では難しい、もしくはエリザベートをもっと楽しみたい！という音楽ファンのみなさまにぜひおすすめしたいのが、Netflix で配信されているドラマ、その名も『皇妃エリザベート』。J.シュトラウス2世がワルツを弾いていたり、当時アイドル的人気を博したリストが宮殿女子から黄色い声を浴びていたり、のちにワグネリアンに成長する少年ルートヴィヒ2世が音楽に夢中になっていたり……と、世界史と音楽史が立体的につながる瞬間がたくさんある。現在シーズン2まで配信されており、最終章となるシーズン3の配信が最近決定。まもなく観られることだろう。 ミュージカル『エリザベート』は、日本では今年から来年にかけて、宝塚歌劇団が上演。「韓国ミュージカル on screen 」も新たなラインナップが発表されており、10月から来年にかけて、注目の3作が上映される予定だ。 舞台からドラマへ、映画、本の世界を経て、また舞台へ……。エリザベート、そして韓国ミュージカルへの熱はしばらくおさまりそうにない。 終演後劇場を出ると、演目のタイトルが映しだされていた 『韓国ミュージカル ON SCREEN』公式サイト 舞台人が語る「WE LOVE MUSICAL!!」第15回 韓国ミュージカル・プロデューサーが語る韓国ミュージカルの楽しみ方 Netflix (﻿ネ﻿ッ﻿ト﻿フ﻿リ﻿ッ﻿ク﻿ス﻿) 『皇妃エリザベート』﻿ EMKミュージカル『ELISABETH』 期間：2026年8月16日 – 2026年11月15日 会場：ブルースクエア ウリ銀行ホール 上演時間：2時間 45分 （休憩時間 20分） 公式サイトはこちら

items.body: 会期：オンライン上映 会場：オンライン上映 公式サイト：https://www.cca.qc.ca/en/events/99570/to-build-law ドキュメンタリー映画『To Build Law』（2024） © CCA. ドイツ人建築家のアルノ・ブランドルフーバーらが、2021年にベルリンで始動した建築設計コレクティブ、bplus.xyz（b+）は、既存建築の境界を解きほぐし、限られた操作によって非建設を成立させる改修・転用を設計活動の軸としている。既存の構造を壊して新たに置き換えるのではなく、そこに残された空間、文脈、素材を読み替える。その抽象的なまでの「建てなさ」は、建築を新たなオブジェクトとして生産するのではなく、すでにあるものとの関係を組み直す行為として捉えたものだ。 こうした実践は物理的なリノベーションにとどまらず、建築環境を規定する法制度そのものを設計対象とした政治的アクティビズムへと展開している。ブランドルーバーもメンバーであるチューリッヒ工科大学のstation.plus（s+）との共同プロジェクト「HouseEurope!」は、解体・新築が選択されやすい制度や評価軸を見直し、既存建築の改修を欧州のスタンダードとして促進するための政治的アクティビズムである。この「HouseEurope!」の舞台裏を描いたドキュメンタリー映画『To Build Law』は、CCA（カナダ建築センター）の映像・展示シリーズ「Groundwork」三部作のひとつとして制作された。そのタイトルが示すように、彼らは建物を建てるのではなく、公開審議によって法を「建てる」（整備する）ことで都市空間を設計しようとしている。 『To Build Law』より。Still from the documentary film To Build Law, 2024 © CCA. 背景にあるのは、世界のCO₂排出量の約38%、総エネルギー消費量の約35%を占めるとされる★1、建築・建設業界の環境負荷の大きさと、建物が生活インフラではなく投機対象として扱われる不動産の金融化への批判である。利潤を追求するスクラップ・アンド・ビルドが加速する一方、多くの都市では住宅不足や価格高騰が深刻化している現実がある。解体・新築を最善とするのではなく、既存建物の価値を見直し、改修や適応型再利用を選択しやすい環境へと転換することが「HouseEurope!」の目標となる。 その手段として用いられるのが、欧州市民イニシアチブ（ECI）という市民発議制度である。EU加盟国のうち7カ国以上から計100万筆以上の署名を集めることで、欧州委員会に立法を提案できるこの制度を活用し、同プロジェクトは、既存建物の改修に関わる税制優遇、EU全域で統一した改修・転用可能性を評価する規則の制定、既存建物の過去のCO₂排出まで対象とするLCA（ライフサイクルアセスメント）の導入などを含む新たな評価枠組みの提案をミッションに掲げる。ボトムアップで法改正を働きかける過程として『To Build Law』が映し出すのは、パートナーシップの形成、市民への呼びかけ、法案の起草、キャンペーン戦略の策定、ロビー活動といった一連のプロセスである。通常は周縁に置かれ目的化しづらい交渉や合意形成といったプロセスが、ここでは建築環境を変革するための設計行為として前景化され、市民へと開かれた構築として示される。 『To Build Law』より。Still from the documentary film To Build Law, 2024 © CCA. 興味深いのは、本作が建築とストーリーテリングを架橋しながら、既存の構造・制度・関係を組み替え、改修を実効性のある手段として開いている点にある。本作ではチューリッヒの建築事務所、Esch Sintzel Architektenがバーゼルで改修した建物が紹介される★2。1955年竣工時のワイン倉庫から配送センターへと用途を変えてきたこの建物は、社会住宅（ソーシャル・ハウジング）への転用にあたり、当初からの構造躯体である巨大な柱とスラブを減築のなかで保存活用することで、コストを抑えつつ新築比42%のグレーエネルギーを節約した。定量的な価値とともに、柱の性格を住空間へと引き継ぐストーリーテリングが演出され、ECIでの提案における実践可能性が示される。 「HouseEurope!」は、2026年1月31日で署名の収集を終了し、約1年間で集まった署名はわずか約8万筆と目標には達成していない。それでも、目に見えない設計のプロセスを建築の前景へと引き出した点に意義を見出せる。建築家の役割は、異なる専門性や市民を結びつけ、空間の変化を生じさせるための条件を構築することへと拡張される。それは都市空間が多様に機能するための、新築の設計・建設だけではない実空間のリノベーションという意味において、今日の生活様式の骨組みをめぐる社会実践と言えるだろう。 この運動から想起されるのは、ヨーゼフ・ボイスが提唱した社会彫刻である。誰もが彫刻家として社会の形成に参加しうると説いたボイスは、「国民投票による直接民主制のための組織」の設立（1971）や、ドクメンタ7を起点に市民とともにカッセル市内へ7000本の樫を植樹した《7000本の樫の木》（1982〜）など、社会や現実を概念的な素材として扱う芸術活動を展開した。対して「HouseEurope!」は、法制度という検証可能な回路を通じた社会参加の試みである。本作が描くのは、都市を構成する物質・空間・人々、そして法規を多くの市民とともに語り直すことの意義と、そのためのプラットフォームおよび方法の更新なのである。 ベルリン、テンペルホーフ空港でのHouseEurope!の集会、2024年。『To Build Law』より。HouseEurope! assembly at Tempelhof Airport, Berlin, 2024. Still from the documentary film To Build Law, 2024 © CCA. ★1──国連環境計画、建築・建設グローバル・アライアンス「建築・建設グローバル環境ステータスレポート2020」（2020） UNEP/GlobalABC “2020 Global Status Report for Buildings and Construction” (2020) https://globalabc.org/resources/publications/2020-global-status-report-buildings-and-construction ★2──『To Build Law』より。https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=61fcc-Gfcz8 『To Build Law』 2024年／49分 原案・構成：フランチェスコ・ガルッティ、アイリーン・チン 監督：ジョシュア・フランク 撮影：アイリス・ン 編集：ケイラ・フラグマン

items.album: 【神奈川】アートと地域をつなぐプログラム　展覧会「庭とキッチン」
items.tags: art sound art contemporary music improvisation
items.excerpt: 横浜・象の鼻テラスにて、アーツコミッション・ヨコハマと、2024年度ACYアーティスト・フェローシップ助成の採択者・永田康祐による展覧会「庭とキッチン」が開催されます。 永田は「地域社会と家庭料理」をテーマに取り組むプロジェクトを行なっており、2026年8月には、コミュニティカフェicocca（横浜市港南区）と、UCHISOTO CAFE（横浜市栄区）で、地域の方々を対象としたワークショップを実施しました。本展では、その記録や参加者へのインタビューをもとに、永田が新作映像作品を制作した成果発表が行なわれます。 本プロジェクトでは、「我が家の味」を共有し、「地元の味」を考えることを通じて、家庭料理や家庭菜園などの暮らしが、地域や社会とどう関わるのかについて考えます。 ＜永田康祐＞ 1990年愛知県生まれ、神奈川県を拠点に活動。近年は、食文化におけるナショナル・アイデンティティの形成や、食事作法における身体技法や権力関係、食料生産における動植物の生の管理といった問題について、ビデオエッセイやコース料理形式のパフォーマンスを発表している。 会期：2026/09/15（火）～2026/09/2

items.body: For the dedicated fans of wind player, composer, and teacher Julius Hemphill, the last two years are shaping up to be an extraordinary era of listening and tribute. Hemphill passed away in 1995 and though he never fell away from the community’s eye, we seem, currently, to be paying much more attention. For a good bit of that,it seems we have Marty Ehrlich to thank. Ehrlich worked with Hemphill and his music over the decades, showing that connection clearly in his own body of work. In 2022 New World released The Boyé Multi-National Crusade For Harmony ( reviewed here ), a 7 disc set of unreleased archival Hemphill recordings, curated by Ehrlich. Now we are presented with Open Air: The Complete Saxophone Quartet Compositions of Julius Hemphill . We don’t need to ask which quartet we’re talking about. Hemphill’s work (along with Oliver Lake, David Murray, and Hamiet Bluett) as a co-founder of the World Saxophone Quartet did not create the sax quartet, but did so much to map its possibilities and implications that it’s hard to imagine how the sax quartet got along before their work. But there’s more. Two thirds of the music Hemphill wrote for sax quartet was recorded by the WSQ, but one third of the music here (14 or so tracks) was discovered in Hemphill’s papers after his death. Ehrlich discovered these while doing archive work with Hemphill’s publisher. It’s somewhat amazing to encounter, 30 years after Hemphill’s death, 14 new pieces for saxophone quartet. It’s like suddenly discovering 14 new Goldberg Variations. (And, no, I do not agree that this is an overwrought analogy. Here’s a bias check for you: there are times when I’m listening to Hemphill’s quartets and I’m completely taken over. In the reverie or ecstasy or elation of those moments, I have been known to think things like, “When God said, let there be music, this is exactly what he was talking about!” I’m not saying I can argue a rational basis for that view, just that sometimes you can look to your elation for a truer kind of truth.) Ehrlich forms a clutch of saxophonists—Allan Chase, Rob Debellis, Brian Landrus, Andy Laster, Jeff Lederer, Lisa Parrott, and Jason Robinson—into a few quartets, recording the whole body of work over a number of months in 2025. The listening is exactly as one would hope. With faithful, passionate, and fascinated renditions of the tunes by musicians who love them, and infused with improvisation that leads to revelation. For example, the WSQ piece, “Revue,” is perhaps the best known sax quartet piece out there, and listening, I can’t help but expect the solo from the WSQ’s second album to come after the statement of the head. It’s a dumb expectation, of course, but Brian Landrus’s solo takes me by surprise and winds along a path that returns to the tune by a way I’ve never been before. The harmonies and ensemble playing of this choir of sax angels can be heart stopping, but the solo on top of those are just as amazing. Ehrlich has shown—particularly on The Hard Blues by his Julius Hemphill Sextet—that he can render the master’s work with skill and authenticity. It’s important because this music is not just interesting and brilliant. It is hard, bluesy, and culturally real as anything you can imagine. It is exactly this mixture of “Stax funk and ‘out’ sensibilities” (to use Tim Berne’s phrase), mixed with an intellectual playfulness, that made Hemphill the composer that he was and keeps me obsessed with his oeuvre thirty years after he’s gone. In case I have to say it, 5 stars. OPEN AIR: The Complete Saxophone Quartet Compositions of Julius Hemphill by Marty Ehrlich Other release... Circle the Heart - Marty Ehrlich and Julius Hemphill (Relative Pitch, 2026) Circle the Heart also explores the saxophone choir space (a duo is a subset of a choir, right?) and gives us insight into the musical collaboration of Hemphill and Ehrlich. The set is a discovered recording of a glorious 1982 concert. Of six tunes, all are Ehrlich compositions save the last, and, in an odd way, this seems only to confirm the shared DNA between the two. Besides, the intrigue is in the improv. The two are so in tune with each other that it’s not enough to call their duo a conversation, so much as a telepathic bonding. Again, I may be over-egging the metaphor, but it really is that good. Circle the Heart by Marty Ehrlich, Julius Hemphill Dogon A.D. - Julius Hemphill (New World Records) Dogon A.D. may be the most cited gateway drug to outmusic of any record out there. The 1972 masterpiece—with its title track in an insanely addictive 11—was re-released in 2011 by International Phonograph. FJB reviewed it here , giving it five stars and listing it as one of the top 20 free jazz recs of all time. That New World is re-releasing it—remastered and co-produced by the ubiquitous Ehrlich—is only good news. I just thought I’d bring it to your attention. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.album: ザ・テンパー・トラップ（The Temper Trap）『Sungazer』オーストラリアのロックバンドが原初的喜びを迸らせる10年ぶりのアルバム

items.body: Label: Nonesuch Records, 2026 Personnel - Henry Threadgill: alto saxophone, flute; Vijay Iyer: piano; Dafnis Prieto: drums. Henry Threadgill, a living legend, avant-garde jazz eminence, and master composer, joins forces with the incredibly creative pianist Vijay Iyer, a reference in modern creative jazz, and proficient Cuban-born drummer Dafnis Prieto, who has worked with Arturo O'Farrill, Eddie Palmieri, and John Zorn. Their debut trio album, Fifteen , comprises a strangely addictive set of post-modern and avant-garde tunes—three by both Threadgill and Iyer, and two by Prieto—that are easily recommended for fans of the three musicians. The album title refers to the number of years the trio has been performing together. Threadgill's " Trio Piece " opens the curtain in a cerebral, slow-chugging way, placing ethereal flute over mystery-inducing piano textures set in the lower register, with understated drumming punctuated by occasional syncopation. If this track gives you an idea of what comes next, " Last Night ", also composed by Threadgill, exceeds our expectations. Boasting a great vibe via its obtuse groove, the piece thrives with forward-leaning drumming, tart saxophone lines, and angular pianism. In the same feral grip of extravagance and sense of groove, Iyer's " I Wanted a Map " mixes structural rock groundwork, avant-garde literacy, and even a bit of Americana. Threadgill blows with soul on the latter, switching to flute on Prieto's " Gently Trapped ", where we can sense a classical innuendo in Iyer's playing. An ethereal flow and an agreeably smooth texture are defining characteristics of this piece. In turn, Iyer's " Fire City " goes from ruminative to ebullient, entering full explorative mode. The theme revealed at the end feels intensely bright yet typified by a few shadowy spots. Blending acute teamwork and killer textures, the trio is free to explore harmonically in the way Iyer envisioned. Yet on his pathos-packed " Perfect Victims ", he rightfully opts for simply arpeggiated sequences that further enhance its elegiac tones. In addition to wailing alto sax, we have timely cymbal washes turned thunderous tom-tom mechanics, providing a ricocheting sense of dynamism at the end. Prieto's " On the Way " packs a wallop, proving the drummer to be a skilled composer. There's a Latin freshness to it, while still bringing out Threadgill's stylistic parameters. Galvanizing percussive work, bustling piano arrays, and terse saxophone expression — all contribute to the hip swagger. This adventurous trio with a distinctly individual vibe certainly has its inventive ways of making its music sound interesting. Fifteen encompasses three strong compositional voices, leading to superior results. Favorite Tracks: 02 - Last Night ► 03 - I Wanted a Map ► 04 - Gently Trapped ► 08 - On the Way

items.body:
Music Matters Live is turning 21, and it is marking the milestone with four nights of free live music in Singapore.

Happening from 2 to 4 October and 7 October at CQ @ Clarke Quay, this year's edition will bring together 40 emerging artists from 15 countries, with performances taking place at Fountain Square, Swee Lee, and more venues around CQ @ Clarke Quay.

The lineup includes Lola Amour from the Philippines, KID PHENOMENON from EXILE TRIBE and LIL LEAGUE from Japan, DOLLA from Malaysia, Borderline from New Zealand, Bratty from Mexico, Pierce Brothers and Flynn Gurry from Australia, Singapore's St. Humain, China's Runyu, and more.

Music Matters Live will also host a series of dedicated showcases throughout the week. Universal Music's Music Is Universal returns on 4 October with performances from DOLLA, LYHAN, MARBLES, VVV, and XONARA, bringing together acts from Malaysia, Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand, and the Philippines.

The festival's MadeIN series will expand with the debut of MadeIN Philippines Spotlight Weekend, presented by NCCA in partnership with BSE and Music Matters. Running from 2 to 4 October, it will feature Filipino acts KAIA, PIX!E, and Lola Amour. MadeIN Japan will bring LIL LEAGUE and KID PHENOMENON to the stage on 3 October, while the inaugural MadeIN Nagaland showcase will spotlight emerging artists from the Indian state.

Meanwhile, Sounds Australia will stage two showcases on 3 and 4 October, featuring Alice George, FVNERAL, Flynn Gurry, Holly Hebe, Lucy Sugerman, Mariae Cassandra, Peach Fuzz, Pierce Brothers, Reuben De Melo, SAHXL, Squid The Kid, and TOWNS.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

Closing out Music Matters Live on 7 October is Girls' Night Out, presented by It's A Girl Thing and Branded. The showcase will feature Bratty — the festival's first artist from Mexico — alongside Maisha Kanna, Lucy Sugerman, SARINA, Singapore's Haneri on the decks, and more. According to the organisers, around half of this year's lineup is female-led.

Music Matters Live will take place alongside the 21st edition of All That Matters, which runs from 5 to 7 October, and forms part of the Singapore Grand Prix Season.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by All That Matters (@matters.asia)

Music Matters Live rundown:

2 October, 6:55 PM — Music Matters Live, Mainstage at Fountain Square

3 October, 4 PM — Music Matters Live / MadeIN Nagaland / MadeIN Philippines Spotlight / MadeIN Japan, Mainstage at Fountain Square

3 October — Sounds Australia @ Swee Lee, Swee Lee @ Clarke Quay

4 October, 4 PM — Music Is Universal, Mainstage at Fountain Square

4 October, 6 PM — Sounds Australia at CQ @ Clarke Quay, Mainstage at Fountain Square

4 October — Music Matters Live, Swee Lee @ Clarke Quay

7 October, 6:45 PM — Girls' Night Out, Mainstage at Fountain Square

7 October — Music Matters Live, Swee Lee @ Clarke Quay

Admission: Free

items.body:
IV OF SPADES are looking for something real on their latest release.

The Filipino alternative quartet have released 'Isang Pag-ibig' via Sony Music Entertainment, a new single that wrestles with the search for genuine connection and the painful realisation that giving someone your all does not necessarily mean they will love you back.

Musically, 'Isang Pag-ibig' keeps things stripped back. Jangly guitars, a three-chord progression, and a straightforward four-piece arrangement give the track a loose and immediate feel, putting its emotional core front and centre. The song was written nearly a decade ago, at the beginning of the band's story, but arrives during a new chapter for the group.

The release follows IV OF SPADES' reunion in late 2025. Unique Salonga, Zild Benitez, Blaster Silonga, and Badjao de Castro have since embarked on their Andalucia Tour, which brought them to Davao City, Santa Rosa, Cagayan de Oro, Cebu City, and Baguio. The band are also set to head to the USA and Canada this October.

Their comeback has also brought renewed attention to earlier material. 'Kabisado' has amassed nearly 80 million Spotify streams, while reaching the top 10 of the Spotify Philippines Daily Chart and peaking at number six on the Billboard Philippines Hot 100.

items.body:
Singapores Grand Prix weekend is about to get a soundtrack from 57 floors up.

Global house act Claptone is set to headline AFTER 2049 on 9 October, taking over the Marina Bay Sands SkyPark Observation Deck for the official closing event of TOKEN2049 Singapore.

Joining Claptone behind the decks is Madrid-based house and tech-house producer Crusy, with ANONM, Leon (FR), Milam, and Mo-Shi completing the night’s lineup.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by AFTER 2049 (@after2049_)

For the occasion, the SkyPark Observation Deck will transform into a limited-capacity party overlooking the city and Formula 1 circuit. Polygon Live will also bring its hemispherical 360° spatial audio system back to the rooftop, marking its only Southeast Asian production of the year.

Claptone is known for his signature golden mask and globe-spanning The Masquerade parties, as well as his Golden Recordings label. Crusy, meanwhile, broke through with his Toolroom debut 'SELECTA' and has since released music via Toolroom, Defected, and Knee Deep In Sound.

“AFTER 2049 returns to the Marina Bay Sands rooftop for Grand Prix weekend with Claptone, 57 floors above the circuit, on the only Polygon rig in Asia this year,” said AFTER 2049 founder Raphael Strauch. “Nothing else comes close.”

To purchase tickets, please visit: https://megatix.com.sg/events/after2049

items.body:
ROSÉ is ready to show fans a 'new trick'.

The BLACKPINK member has teased her upcoming solo single which is set to arrive on 17 September at 7 PM ET. The track will be accompanied by a music video directed by Dave Meyers and filmed entirely on Apple's newly unveiled iPhone 18 Pro.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by apple (@apple)

A teaser shared by ROSÉ and Apple offers a brief preview of the track, with the singer holding a purple-burgundy lollipop wrapped with the words "new trick". Sonically, the snippet introduces distorted electric guitar and layered vocals, hinting at a punchier side to ROSÉ's solo sound.

The release also marks ROSÉ's appearance in Apple's latest Shot on iPhone campaign. Previous instalments have featured music videos from The Weeknd, Olivia Rodrigo, and Lady Gaga.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by apple (@apple)

Meyers, who has previously directed music videos for Taylor Swift, Harry Styles, and Kendrick Lamar, helmed the upcoming visual using the iPhone 18 Pro's camera system.

'new trick' follows ROSÉ's debut studio album, rosie, released in December 2024. The record featured her Bruno Mars collaboration 'APT.', which peaked at number three on the Billboard Hot 100.

items.excerpt: Washington, D.C. experimental label ZeroMoon has published its Best of August 2026 playlist, a seven-track, 66-minute survey of “obscure, obtuse, and overlooked” releases. The set moves through drone, noise, free improvisation, electroacoustic music, and other experimental territory, with selections from Šimanský Vaľko Podracký, Cedrik Fermont, Diurnal Burdens, Tim Olive, Gentle Fire, Irene Aranda, and LULE.
