items.body: One has to admire the boldness of the opening of Cacciamali. It doesn’t try to dazzle; instead, it opts for understated playfulness. A faltering folk wind instrument sets the tone as if the player were testing it rather than performing on it. This is not an artist trying to impress but someone searching. Rosso Polare introduces the album as an act of exploration. The hesitant breaths soon give way to rougher growls before the music gathers momentum through the increasingly insistent drumming of Cinna Peyghamy’s tombak. “Falò” immediately shifts the atmosphere. Beginning with recordings from a bonfire, the track slowly thickens until a guitar emerges from the electroacoustic fabric, introducing one of the album’s rare melodic moments. Its simple folk-like phrase briefly offers a point of orientation before gradually dissolving back into the surrounding texture. Equally striking are the barely audible voices: “la carezza di un ricordo… il rifiuto di un ventre… il rifiuto di una madre… il rifiuto di un figlio…” (“the caress of a memory… the rejection of a womb… the rejection of a mother… the rejection of a son…”). There is no explanation and no obvious narrative. The words are uttered almost like a spell. That reluctance to foreground melody becomes one of the album’s defining characteristics. Even when recognisable instrumental gestures appear, they are never allowed to establish themselves as fixed themes. They emerge briefly before being reabsorbed into a constantly shifting ensemble in which electronics, acoustic instruments and environmental recordings occupy the same musical plane. The collaborations expand this vocabulary without disrupting its coherence. Riccardo Sinigaglia’s presence introduces a subtle dialogue between electronic abstraction and ritual memory. “Monte” overlays dense electronic textures with ritualistic drumming, children’s voices and the distant bells of grazing animals, creating a landscape that feels inhabited rather than merely observed. “Hastilude” — named after the medieval martial games derived from hasta (spear) and ludus (play) — is one of the album’s thickest sonic environments, its layers continually reshaping one another without ever settling into stable hierarchies. “1744”, created with HMOT (Stas Shärifulla), opens in an almost cinematic manner, or perhaps like the score to a contemporary dance piece, before gradually giving way to the denser electronic textures that characterise the album’s second half. The liner notes provide an illuminating framework without dictating how the music should be heard. Side A draws upon the rhythmic traditions of medieval quintain games and flag throwing, while Side B is structured around a local legend recounting a fatal duel between father and son in 1744. Yet Rosso Polare avoids illustrating either narrative. Instead, ritual and rupture become compositional principles: repetition gradually gives way to fracture, while tradition quietly coexists with loss. Equally important is the album’s treatment of place and everyday life. No location is identified, yet the accents of the spoken voices suggest northern Italy, while one overheard remark hints that the recordings were made shortly before Christmas. These details are never highlighted; they simply exist alongside the music. In “La Cruma”, snippets of perfectly intelligible conversation drift in and out of the texture without carrying any obvious symbolic meaning. They are not clues to be deciphered but reminders that this music belongs to inhabited places. Throughout the album, field recordings never function as scenic decoration. They remain part of the same sonic fabric as the instruments and electronics. That approach has characterised Rosso Polare’s work from the beginning. Whether in Lettere Animali, Bocca d’Ombra or Campo Amaro — whose “Testamento Fermo” includes an impromptu chorus formed by those present — his music has consistently embraced participation over authorship. Cacciamali is the first album released after the departure of Anna Vezzosi, yet it continues this collective ethos. Collaboration is never ornamental; it is embedded in the way the music is conceived. The title itself, Cacciamali (“chasing away evils”), inevitably recalls Ernesto de Martino’s studies of ritual and popular belief in southern Italy, particularly La terra del rimorso, alongside Diego Carpitella’s groundbreaking field recordings documenting music as a means of confronting suffering and uncertainty. Rosso Polare never quotes those traditions directly, but he seems to share an ethnomusicologist’s curiosity. His music occupies a space where free improvisation, folk memory and traces of pagan ritual coexist without hierarchy. Whistling, traditional flutes, environmental sound, electronics and percussion are granted equal importance, while the natural world and human presence continually overlap. Rather than reconstructing folklore, Cacciamali uncovers the fragile traces it leaves behind, allowing stories, landscapes and communities to emerge through listening rather than explanation. To paraphrase Alice in Wonderland, “What is the use of music with no pictures or conversations?” Cacciamali has both in sonic form. Rosso Polare photo courtesy the artist To find out more on how to chase away evils, I reached out to Rosso Polare for an interview conducted by email, after which I followed up with a couple of clarifications. One of the things I found most compelling about Cacciamali is that it never separates music from the world around it. Environmental recordings, recognisable human voices and fragments of everyday conversations continually drift in and out of the texture. They never function as documentary material, but neither do they become anonymous sound objects. Instead, they anchor the music within a living environment. How do you approach the relationship between field recordings and instrumental sound? At what point does an environmental recording stop being documentation and become part of the composition? Since the beginning of Rosso Polare, the threshold between environmental recording and tonal sound has always been some sort of challenge. In the project’s body of work, field recordings are simply treated as integral sonic material within the composition, and it’s more a matter of a mental shift: giving the same relevance to material that could generally be seen as background, and striving to put it on the same level as composed sound. On the other hand, it’s also about stepping down with regard to played music: treating it, as much as possible, as if it were a “piece of the story” rather than the highlight of the specific musician who played it. This very difficult proposition is an attempt to make these two distinct habitats coexist without one being preponderant over the other. When does an environmental recording stop being documentation? I guess it happens in a very gradual way for me, as I gather sounds with no particular structure in mind in the first place and then assemble them afterward in the studio. Though I usually tend to avoid modern human anthropophony, it’s only with the last two albums, Campo Amaro and Cacciamali, that Rosso Polare started to embrace a bit of that as well. Before that, the project leaned away from the human voice in order to make the pieces feel as “in and out of this world” as possible, I would say. On these two albums, on the other hand, there’s some sort of investigation into folklore inside me that still has something to say, I think. So yes, as I gather sounds, they start to become part of a bigger picture, but they are always treated as just sounds, in much the same way that I treat instruments. I recently spoke to Cinna Peyghamy, who described improvisation as “moderating a debate between two very different speakers.” Listening to “XIV – Pavo”, that image immediately came to mind. He brings multiphonics and an extraordinary physicality to the opening track, yet they seem to become part of a much larger sonic organism rather than taking centre stage. What attracted you to Cinna’s approach to sound, and how did the dialogue between the two of you shape the identity of the piece? I met Cinna a while back in Basel. At the time, Rosso Polare was still a duo and we were playing at Würm on the very same night as him. Stas Shärifulla, a very good friend and artist I greatly admire, had invited both acts to play, and we almost instantly connected. I really like Cinna’s quote here and find it very fitting in this conversation too. “xiv – pavo” is the opening piece of what is, for me, a very difficult album, an album about balancing both music and personal emotions, making peace with changing aspects of my life. Thematically, it started with the concept of quintain games, flag throwing specifically, as the main melodic column is made of environmental recordings from a flag-throwing game in Spoleto, which, uncommonly these days, featured horns alongside the classic drumming. Once back in the studio, I mangled these recordings into rhythmic patterns, and the horns that came with them got weird in a very interesting way: rather than resembling a specific melody, they became some sort of average fantasy of Italian folk music, not as a cliché but more out of a damaged memory, I’d say. Alongside that came what I’d describe as embracing my limitations: between starting and finishing the recording, I contracted a severe form of pneumonia, which highly affected my lung capacity and, subsequently, my ability to play wind instruments for long periods. Lots of whispers, pants, breath struggles and inhaled screams were sampled and implemented as assets to the track rather than obstacles in the process. Cinna’s drumming and modular processing added great counterpoint to the already complex patterns of the track, while also grounding the second part of the piece in a more upfront dimension of musicality. His command of the tombak is really beyond anyone I’ve had the chance to listen to, and the integration of this very tactile instrument with modular synthesis is as difficult as it gets. I felt this track was a fitting opportunity to collaborate. He received from me what was, at the time, a somewhat finished part, and the dialogue started from that. You know, how do you integrate your voice into this? What and when should you play? Stylistic questions more than technicalities, I think, ideas about the shape of the music. The role of this track as an opener was really hard to frame in the first place. The one before was an album about Italian folk traditional chants and their potential for a modern adaptation, and I still thought that thread had to be developed in some way, so that’s when the quintain came in. But, in parallel, I came across a local legend about a son dueling with his father and being fatally struck in 1744 in Lombardy, which sort of acted as a hidden subtext throughout the record, picking up this sense of loss and despair I felt while finishing the album. So “xiv – pavo“ is basically an introduction to a specific habitat for me. One aspect I found particularly interesting is that Cacciamali brings together musicians who already share artistic connections. For instance, as a curator of the Korkut Triennale, Stas Shärifulla (HMOT) invited Cinna Peyghamy to perform while Riccardo Sinigaglia comes from an entirely different generation of Italian electronic music. Rather than sounding like a collection of guest appearances, the album feels like the meeting point of several different experimental music communities. Was that network of relationships something you consciously wanted to bring together, and did those existing connections influence the way the collaborations developed? Firstly, all appearances on the record are either friends or musicians I met and shared a vision with. Stas, with his wife Julia, was part of the label (Klammklang, now inactive) that published Rosso Polare’s first album, Lettere Animali, in 2020. We’ve been friends ever since, and I was really happy to finally collaborate on something in the studio. Cinna Peyghamy, as said before, has been a staple connection since the show in Basel and resonated both in ideas and music. Riccardo Sinigaglia is the unsung hero of experimental underground music in Italy since the ’80s. I fell in love with the debut of his band, Futuro Antico, a stunning example of cosmic experimentation that went beyond Italian music at the time. We met back in 2021 at Bääfest in Milano and connected. For me, his appearance on the record is a way to continue something that happened closer to me, a sort of homage to my musical ancestry, in a way. The beauty of this scene is the possibility of bringing together communities, as you suggested: having friends representing different scenes of experimental music and making the ends meet altogether, be it on recorded media or live performances. This network is something you build along the way through true bonds and experiences. In Cacciamali, the aim was to bring together, on record, this friendship and kin built along the way. Throughout the album I had the impression that you compose less by arranging sounds than by allowing them to find relationships with one another. Even the improvised pieces display an extraordinary sense of formal control, while the more structured works never lose their spontaneity. I’m curious about your working process. When you’re developing a piece, what tells you that it has reached its final form? Is it a question of balance, density, resonance, or is there another criterion you rely on before deciding that nothing more needs to be added—or taken away? My process relies heavily on spontaneity, followed by very meticulous arranging which, as you rightly pointed out, strives to find relationships and conversation between them. I like to think of my pieces as chapters of a book or acts in a movie. Even though it’s usually not that pondered in the recording stage, I start with a few ideas. Lately, it’s more about a series of “what ifs”: “What if this melody idea goes on top of this field recording?” or “What if I record this sound in this way?” or “What if I prepare a guitar with these objects?” etc. I don’t really like to know the themes of my works at the start. At the same time, I know when I’m working on a series of tracks that will be part of a whole, and I like to think that the themes and concepts I later find words for were actually inside the sounds all along. So it’s more like extracting what I’m trying to say from the music itself. I’d say lately it’s become more common for me to have a few stories or loose thoughts in mind at the start. Then there’s a very long time that I spend rearranging and mixing, continuously questioning myself, the tracks and sounds inside, but in a properly healthy way. I’m very picky, to the point that I even annoy myself at times, so it’s a bit of a struggle. Part of me wants to get the most out of the record, but I still need to fight this race for perfection, as it’s easy to lose a fair bit of spontaneity in the music. I always want it to feel slightly rough and to retain a sense of momentum as well. When a piece has reached its final form? Fearing here that I might sound a bit trivial, but for me it’s also a matter of gut feeling. My role is to serve the music, much as a messenger serves his purpose, and I try to sense when my part is done. Usually, a piece is ready when it feels like it’s become part of the story as a whole, when it’s telling its part of the album and feels worthy of its conversation. As a follow up, since you mentioned you had pneumonia, so did you play the flute one can hear at the very beginning of the album while recovering? The flute playing at the beginning is the only flute I don’t play. I recorded it in Switzerland at the Goetheanum. On a hill, there was a man playing a sort of Buffalo Horn. I was with Stas, curiously enough. All the other flutes on the album, however, are mostly bamboo, very rough-hewn, both transverse and with traditional mouthpieces. I think there’s also a metal transverse flute at times, and a couple of recorders, of two different sizes (soprano and tenor, I think). From the pneumonia period, the wind instruments featured are mainly the simplest to play, the small ones that require less air, plus, of course, the various reworked rattles you hear. Finally, could you confirm that the voices one can hear in the track “la cruma” were recorded in Lombardy in northern Italy? Exactly, the “Cruma” recordings come from the province of Lombardy. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: This is what it sounds like when a producer has a large collection of morning keyboard improvisations, a practice the artist calls “Chaos Works,” recorded daily as a meditative exercise, and decides to present them honestly rather than sculpting them into something more conventionally structured. A brainstorming session that stays comfortable in its own incompleteness memoryleaks (([||])) by You Us We Them   CONDUIT—stylized as CONDU||T—is a Los Angeles-based creative collective and label operating under the ethos “how we shape the world is what the world becomes.” Since at least 2022, the collective has been releasing electronic, experimental, ambient, and downtempo music across a roster that includes Left/Right, canary yellow, Scaefa, and You Us We Them, donating a portion of proceeds from compilation releases to causes including Doctors Without Borders and hunger relief in Palestine. It’s a label with genuine community intent, and memoryleaks arrives as its most ambitious and personal release yet, a debut full-length from You Us We Them, the LA composer and visual artist whose previous work appeared scattered across CONDUIT compilation releases. 31 tracks. The first thing to establish is what to call them, not tracks in the conventional sense, but mini excerpts, ideas, fragments. Some are interludes, some are fully formed concepts, and others sound like good ideas that could have been built into something larger but weren’t. That’s not a criticism so much as an observation about intent. This is what it sounds like when a producer has a large collection of morning keyboard improvisations, a practice the artist calls “Chaos Works,” recorded daily as a meditative exercise, and decides to present them honestly rather than sculpting them into something more conventionally structured. Some of them could have expanded into larger compositions. Maybe that’s the point. Maybe they’re comfortable exactly where they sit. The melodies are the strongest element throughout and the clearest standout across all 31 pieces. The synth selection and mild effects being applied make this a beauty to listen to, bending toward ambient and experimental throughout. Comparisons to Geogaddi by Boards of Canada surface naturally, that album specifically, minus the drum work. Pure melodic bliss without rhythmic infrastructure, which leaves the melodic ideas fully exposed and either beautiful or insufficient depending on what’s underneath them. Here, what’s underneath is personal, real audio recordings collaged from childhood films, tape, and cell phone videos. A marriage proposal. Voicemails. Conversations with people no longer here. That material is embedded throughout and when it surfaces it changes the weight of everything surrounding it. Some of the darker melodic compositions and bass synth selections carry traces of Lorn‘s specific brand of dark, heavy note choices, that same gravity applied to what might otherwise float away into pure ambience. A fragment of a memory plot executed with genuine intent :: The track naming deserves attention because it rewards close reading. Usually when producers name tracks abstractly you expect the connection between title and content to be decorative rather than meaningful. Here the intent is visible. “memoryleak_non-duality”—27 seconds, is a mixture of recordings and field recordings ending with what sounds like a voicemail of a child saying “I love you.” The piece feels like someone accessing a series of memories rapidly and landing on one specific moment. The connection between title and content clicks immediately and the impact of that 27-second piece lands harder than many tracks ten times its length. “down below” applies a bouncing effect to melodies that are slowly fading and dying in sound, you can hear what sounds like seagulls or a beach setting beneath it, at least that’s what surfaces in the listening. The “memoryleak” prefixed tracks function as a distinct subcategory throughout the album, strange glimpses of something not supposed to be accessed, each one a fragment of a memory plot executed with genuine intent. A technical note worth making: a lot of the melodic structures on this album are heavily compressed. In experimental and ambient music, compression applied aggressively to melodic content does something specific, it reduces the dynamic range, bringing the quieter moments up and pushing the louder moments down until everything sits at a similar level. The effect can create a dreamlike, smeared quality where notes seem to float without natural attack and decay, which suits the memory-as-medium concept of this album perfectly. What sounds like a technical limitation is actually a compositional choice that reinforces the album’s core idea, memories don’t have natural dynamic range either. They arrive at whatever volume your mind decides, flattened or amplified by emotional association rather than actual acoustic level. “memoryleak_harbinger” is the favorite of that batch, a build that makes it feel like something epic is about to happen, then never delivers it. A woman humming, building, connecting her melodic humming to what sounds like an orchestral swell, only for it to fade and disintegrate in bitrate at the end. It is pure sound design work and a wonderful 30 seconds of listening. The album closes with “Give It Time (Life Theme)” and “rebmemeR (end is the beginning),” teasing, strange, unfinished feeling. But that’s what this album is supposed to be: an intentionally unfinished process of raw and pure melodies, a brainstorming session that stays comfortable in its own incompleteness. One thought that kept surfacing while listening: this material would make an extraordinary remix album. The melodic DNA here is strong enough that handing these fragments to other artists, from inside the CONDUIT roster or outside it, and letting them build full compositions around them feels like an obvious and genuinely exciting next step. Whether that ever happens or not, memoryleaks works exactly as it is—raw, personal, and comfortable in its own incompleteness in a way that takes real confidence to pull off. memoryleaks is a 31-track collection of short vignettes woven together with actual memories: real audio recordings from childhood films, tape recordings, and cell phone videos. His proposal to his wife, conversations with family no longer here, and voicemails from friends are all layered within. It is deeply personal. memoryleaks (([||])) is available on CONDUIT. [Bandcamp] The post You Us We Them :: memoryleaks (([||])) (CONDU||T) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: To accompany his article on Aspen Edities in The Wire 512, Peter Margasak compiles an annotated playlist of tracks from the Belgium label There’s nothing unusual about the fact that Belgian guitarist Ruben Machtelinckx started a label to release his own music. But as his Aspen Edities imprint approaches its tenth anniversary next year, the scope of the project has steadily, if quietly, expanded and changed. The label’s carefully curated catalogue has chronicled that development release by release, with almost every subsequent title carving out fresh terrain while simultaneously honouring its meditative but exploratory roots. The following playlist explores Aspen Edities’ subtly shifting outlook. Christian Wallumrød Ensemble “New hum old hum” From Non Sonett (2026) Pointing to the ECM roots of the Christian Wallumrød Ensemble is too simple. While Aspen Edities label runner Machtelinckx loves the label, the singular collision of indelible, old fashioned chamber melodies and harmonically focused expanses of sustained sound in the pianist/composer’s music feels like the stronger connection. Wallumrød continues an instinctual engagement with electronics, offering a built-on contrast when placed next to the rustic church music feel, and, as heard on the adroitly titled “New hum old hum”, explores tiptoeing gauzy timbral clouds fed through the prism of alternate tunings. Machtelinckx/Badenhorst/Cools/Gouband“Structure 6” From Porous Structures (2019) In some way the arc of the Aspen Edities’ aesthetic can be traced through Machtelinckx’s own work. This richly atmospheric quartet recording features his guitar playing clinging to vestiges of his jazz roots, with shades of Ralph Towner emanating from his interplay with fellow guitarist Bert Cools (Merope). The sui generis sound world of French drummer Tomas Gouband, who prefers to employ tree branches and stones rather than brushes and sticks on his kit, carves out a thick resonance, amplified by generous reverb, while the great Belgian artist Joachim Badenhorst toggles between liquid clarinet melodies and wordless vocals, à la Arve Henriksen. Graden/Agnas/Landin/Bromander “Chimär” From Words Were Coming Out Of Our Ears (2025) The label tapped into the Swedish scene earlier this year with this superb quartet, in which bassists Pär Ola Landen and Vilhelm Bromander actively swap and double up on roles, adding melody and fracturing time within a sub-internal dialogue. The drowsy tempos, laid out with exquisite elasticity by drummer Nils Agnas, and harmonically draped by the feather stroke touch of pianist Johan Graden, loosely evoke the legacy of fellow Scandinavian drummer Jon Christensen and pianist Bobo Stenson, but they inject a more contemporary elegant concision and directness. Dans Les Arbres “les yeux écoutent” From L’Album Vert (2024) The French-Norwegian quartet Dans Les Arbes have carved out a beguiling world of sustained tones and elusive textures on its recordings for ECM, Hubro and Sofa, but they found a simpatico landing spot for L’Album Vert, which maintains a meticulous rigour and attention to detail while embracing the fresh presence of electronic gestures and irregular rhythmic disruptions. Percussionist Ingar Zach, pedal steel guitarist Ivar Grydeland, clarinetist Xavier Charles and keyboardist Christian Wallumrød all possess extended timbral vocabularies, but they function as a single organism. Linus & BPB “Little Jesus, Mighty God” From The Outside, The Music Of Jules De Corte (2026) This new album reinforces the label’s unpredictability and breadth, as Machtelinckx’s longtime project with reedist Thomas Jillings takes a left turn into pop territory. Joined by frequent collaborator Fredrik Leroux and bassist Laurens Smet, the group interprets a selection of tunes by the once popular but now overlooked Jules de Corte, the blind Dutch singer-songwriter and pianist. Jillings translated the lyrics into English and the delicate guitar-centric arrangements make a perfect fit for the gorgeous singing of Bonnie 'Prince' Billy, who helps transform the repertoire, giving it a timeless warmth. Poor Isa “Ply” From Poor Isa + Evan Parker/Ingar Zach (2025) Machtelinckx and frequent cohort Fredrik Leroux started Poor Isa to experiment with some very unusual instrumentation: banjos and woodblocks. Through various extended techniques and the use of e-bows the project has developed a surprisingly broad soundworld, as if some bluegrass pickers were trading fours with a gagaku ensemble. A collaboration with the veteran British saxophonist Evan Parker seemed just as odd, but with the help of regular collaborator, Norwegian percussionist and sound artist Zach, they reveal a shape-shifting versatility. Oker “Crepuscular Rays” From Aerial (2026) This sublime Norwegian group entered the Aspen Edities fold through its Berlin based guitarist Fredrik Rasten, who collaborated with Machtelinckx on his hypnotising solo album Strands Of Lunar Light, a collection of serene experiments in just intonation. Oker got its start composing delicate, folk inspired compositions heavily informed by the improvisational backgrounds of percussionist Jan-Martin Gismervik, bassist Adrian Fiskum Myhr and trumpeter Torstein Lavik Larsen, but over time an attraction to spontaneity has led them to construct their pieces in real time, which Aerial captures. Still, the ensemble builds these delicate, detail-rich extended excursions with structure in mind. Veder“Sedum” From Evergreen (2017) Released in 2017, this is one of the earliest Aspen Edities titles, offering a sonic blueprint that can be connected to many of its recent releases. Machtelinckx’s calmly unfolding guitar and banjo serves as a perfect foil for the unusual braid of horns provided by Norwegian trumpeter Eivind Lønning, Belgian reedist Joachim Badenhorst, and Belgian euphonium player Niels Van Heertum, who composed these stately themes. The music is gentle but introspective, transmitting an unusual strain of chamber jazz that erases any division between extended techniques, contrapuntal elegance, and melodic generosity. Read Peter Margasak’s full Unlimited Editions column on Aspen Edities in The Wire 512. Wire subscribers can also read the article online via the digital magazine library.

items.body: Four years ago Intibint started making a record she wasn’t sure anyone would fund. Last July she threw a fundraiser for it on her own birthday, at The Rum Shack in Glasgow’s Southside with the Arab club night WSHWSH, and told the room that the politics in her work might cost her the grant she was applying for. She got there in the end, politics and all: Half Moon Eyes comes out on 18 September through Bandcamp and SoundCloud and nowhere else, played live first at Ormside Projects in London tomorrow and Stereo in Glasgow on Saturday. Born in London, raised between there and Sanaa and now in Glasgow, she wrote the album across Yemen, Egypt, Slovakia, England and Scotland and produced, recorded and mixed every part of it herself. Travelling, she records what she hears: that’s how trains, fireworks and dolphins from those journeys run through “Dolphin”, gunshots from Yemeni celebration footage inside “Disrespectful af”, a Glasgow trans rights protest from 2025 opening “S.A.B.R”. “Disrespectful af” was built out of an argument in which she was called disrespectful for naming racism, and “Hayati”, the one song out before release, came from working out in Glasgow that a Yemeni woman could live a life for herself. She sings in Arabic and English across the album, close to the microphone, repeating her lines, over nocturnal pop chords and production that moves between downtempo, alt-R&B, grime and EBM, with Arabic modal writing under most of it. Live, she performs from CDJs most nights, though for these two launches three musicians join her on stage. Ekin Oykener, the Cypriot musician who plays oud on the album’s “Sunflower” and “S.A.B.R”, takes guitar and oud, and Fatma Hegazy, an Egyptian-Scottish artist trained on classical guitar who also DJs at both nights, takes the other guitar, completing the line-up with Nadine on drums. Between her own songs she reaches for revolutionary ones from Yemen, Palestine and Sudan. Tomorrow’s London show is put on by grassroots promoter flowers.ldn with WSHWSH, at Ormside Projects. The arts centre has run out of a unit in the Penarth Centre off Old Kent Road since 2015, Arts Council funded, showing films, mounting exhibitions and listening parties, running workshops and a photography studio, and handing the room over most weekends to independent promoters working the experimental end of electronic music: industrial and deconstructed club, dub techno, gqom and hard drum, footwork and jungle. flowers.ldn and WSHWSH are behind Saturday’s show too, at Stereo in Glasgow, which took over the ground floor and basement of Mackintosh’s Daily Record building on Renfield Lane in 2007. A vegan cafe bar runs upstairs and the gigs happen in the space below, programmed heavily towards queer and marginalised artists and the experimental end of club music: dubstep and grime, jungle and drum and bass, baile funk, ballroom, MENA and SWANA club nights. Four DJs play both nights, either side of the live set. Salam Kitty co-founded WSHWSH after starting the Scottish QTIPoC+ party Mojxmma, and plays bass-heavy percussive club music with Afro-electro and leftfield techno in it. Nihal El Aasar grew up in Cairo, writes from London, and spends her monthly NTS show Nile to Bank following left-field hip hop, drill and drum and bass out of the Middle East and North Africa. MAVEEN and Fatma Hegazy fill out both bills, Fatma opening tonight before she picks up the guitar later, with candice a.m in London and unknown niece, who co-created flowers.ldn, in Glasgow. Half Moon Eyes is out on the 18th, but you can hear it live first: Ormside tomorrow, doors at 7pm with Intibint on at 21:20, then Stereo on Saturday from half nine. Nobody gets turned away for lack of funds, so if you are on Universal Credit, seeking asylum or just short, message the promoters and you are on the door.   Tickets are on sale for tomorrow in London and Saturday in Glasgow   The post Event Preview: Intibint @ Ormside Projects (London; Thursday 10th September 2026) & Stereo (Glasgow; Saturday 12th September 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: An off-kilter rhythm out of West African highlife opens “Higher Levels”, and Bart Vervaeck‘s guitar threads thin microtonal lines through it that lean towards Malian desert blues, while Lieven Van Pée‘s bass bubbles beneath in a funk register. It is the second single from Collective Intelligence, the third album from Brussels quartet Echoes of Zoo, out on 2 October via Rebel Up! Records and Zephyrus Records. The quartet formed in 2018 around saxophonist and composer Nathan Daems, who also leads Ethio-jazz five-piece Black Flower. Vervaeck and drummer Falk Schrauwen play in Ghent psych-jazz collective Compro Oro, Van Pée in jazz trio De Beren Gieren. Since the 2019 EP First Provocations, through BREAKOUT in 2021 and Speech of Species in 2023, they have built a punk-edged psychedelic jazz on Middle Eastern microtonal melody and West African rhythm. Animals have set the terms for each record: BREAKOUT on the friction between humans and animals, Speech of Species on how species talk to one another, this one on how they move as a single body. The album’s second track is called “Wolf Pack Telepathy”, and Daems ties the “Higher Levels” title to the sophisticated ways animals communicate and coordinate as one, or “what we casually call telepathy, though that label says more about our own limits than what’s actually possible in nature.” Stream “Higher Levels” and pre-order Collective Intelligence HERE The post Daily Discovery: Echoes of Zoo – Higher Levels appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Being a robust rebel is fully explained by my Prog Rogue moniker and there is no intention ever to alter that mindset. Receiving music from any hitherto unknown musician often reveals somewhere along the line a few connections, whether in style, in associations or guest artists. It was therefore easy to agree to getting the download done when the name Rob Harrison from Z Machine showed up in the EPK. Lester drums for that band. Bingo! The dots are connected. Even though my personal prog shrine remains deeply entrenched in melodic and symphonic stylistics, there is no way that I would contemplate not tasting material outside of the comfort zone I am most familiar with. In fact, recently dabbling in dungeon synth artists, darkwave, and folk-metal as well as continuously listening to jazz, experimental and electronic provide a very wide berth of interest. This release typically required an initial listen to reformulate the ears into an altogether different mindset and a third revisit confirmed my thoughts as well as dispelling any misgivings. The Rogue enjoys being challenged, musically and otherwise. Sometimes thought-provoking music can come across as masturbatory displays of ego-driven chopzilla (as I witnessed sadly at a 1973 Return to Forever concert, opening for Focus of all people, and Stanley Clarke's spot was so crass that the devout fans started booing him). This is absolutely not the case anywhere on this album. Let us dive in, so to speak. "Anaraknophobia" could very well be a fear of spiders that thrive in a polar anorak , only Lester knows for sure. This is a great introductory piece that combines sturdy bass playing, brass instruments and electric guitars , as well as the percussive talents of the man in question, providing some vibraphone inserts as well . Its very modern jazz, with overt influences of that glorious Brit jazz-rock school I particularly cherish with well-heeled names like Soft Machine, Hatfield and the North, Nucleus, Neil Ardley, Gilgamesh, Penguin Caf� Orchestra, In Cahoots, Catapilla, Blue Drift, Turning Point, Back Door and many others. So let that sink in before plunging headfirst into the colossal maelstrom that is the title track, a nearly 22-minute behemoth of bedazzling authority, stunning contrasts, roller coaster rides well within the free jazz lineage. It's a master class of impeccable musicianship on a collective basis being the core strength attribute of jazz but where the solo spots are deeply entangled within the endless succession of variations, shifts, moods and atmospheres, every player taking a turn with the ball. Needless to state that this performance is worthy of the loftiest praise, placing this arrangement, an undeniably accurate comment may I add , on the same altar ruled by the previously mentioned stalwarts. The immediate impression is one of a sonic mosaic composed of a myriad of little details that interlock perfectly like an Inca jigsaw puzzle, a cinematographic soundtrack that may leave one confounded but never confused. Close your eyes, open your ears and imagine a place where speed, silk, swing, serenity, stupefaction race along the canals of your mind, finished off by a niggling hint of argy-bargy (i.e my favourite British word), rekindling a kind recollection of a Rob Harrison album title called "Explode My Head" ! Where the hell is my jaw, I can't seem to find it anymore ! And to blur the issue even further, "Moonfire" is a giant leap sideways into more ambient realms, influenced by that classic SM track off Softs "Song of Aeolus", a pastoral promenade that glitters gently like a sunny day in Albion, a gorgeous melodic asteroid of celestial joy, unpretentiously pretty and heartfelt. Really worth holding onto. Thanks to an unexpected typo (are they not always unforeseen?), "Worth Holding Onto" has a garrulously rumbling bass leading the way, galloping all over the green valleys and glimmering meadows, with more stop and starts than a failing computer. Utterly playful, especially for a bass fanatic like me, I literally got off on this track, what a ride. The melodicism surfaces once again on "Joining the Q", a line that dares to go around the entire block, keeping the easy-going patients entertained as they await their turn. The super cool vibraphone spot comes in to wink at the crowd, the bass burping delectably, and Lester doing his Buddy Rich thingy, shuffles and ruffles galore. Just when one feels comfortable in getting the true meaning of an album, Lester takes this once again into a "Mountain Pass", a short sonic slash between peaks that has the audacity to combine Celtic bliss with rapid-fire percussive agility! That's right folks, it's his mini-solo spotlight! Fabulous. Finishing in style with a funky dispatch and perhaps waving mean polkadot handkerchiefs "Mister Meaner" has all the urban charm of a vivacious late afternoon romp around the various sites and sound of happy place, everyone smiling and content with the niceties of life (like great music). That insistent bass has totally seduced me, I must admit, I think I have fallen in love. The breezy keys, the daring electric guitar solo and the brass work are all the added spice one can ask for. And now, for the coup de grace (Pronounced "koo de grass" for you anglophiles ): all the instrumentation, recording , arranging and producing was undertaken by one Lester Greenhalgh . Golden buzzer. 4.5 hard machines

items.body: Review by andrea — "Mass-Media Stars" is the second album by Acqua Fragile and was released in 1974 on the Ricordi label with a confirmed line up featuring Bernardo Lanzetti (vocals, guitar), Gino Campanini (electric and acoustic guitar, vocals), Maurizio Mori (keyboards, vocals), Franz Dondi (bass) and Pier Emilio Canavera (drums, acoustic guitar, vocals). The album, produced by Claudio Fabi (best known for his work with PFM), has a good sound quality and the musicians seem more aware of their songwriting abilities. In my opinion, the tracks on it sound more personal and mature if compared with those on their self-titled debut. However, the final outcome is somewhat hampered by the band's stubbornness in insisting on singing their songs in English, against the wishes of their record company and an Italian market that was at the time unreceptive to such a proposal. This led to a commercial flop, despite the quality of the album...The fine opening track, "Cosmic Mind Affair", evokes astronomical laws that serve as a guide for our minds, inviting us on a journey into the depths of the cosmos while walking on the thin line of madness. The mysteries of the universe are too profound to be fathomed or understood by our limited human capabilities: what if we were nothing more than strange, incredible creatures generated by the brains of other worlds? Like the aliens that populate our dreams...The following "Bar Gazing" is at times musically reminiscent of Genesis while its somewhat surreal lyrics draw inspiration from the observation of the customers of a bar located in a town square. An unruly driver, a bee inspector, a couple of pharmacy lovers...The instrumental intro to "Mass-Media Stars" is strongly reminiscent of PFM. Then, the festive atmosphere is paired with sarcastic lyrics about rock stars and their diva-like attitudes: vain artists who bark loudly in the air, with a political touch and the gift of the gab; frivolous Lolitas who think they can do rock'n'roll better than Elvis while flaunting a thousand gimmicks that you have to admire with the blessing of the media..."Opening Act" starts by a vocal part a cappella that might bring Gentle Giant to mind, but the music soon shifts toward a West Coast sound. The track brilliantly and wryly depicts life on the road for an obscure rock band trying to make a name for itself by opening the concerts for major stars. There are no press clippings about the unknown band, no groupies waiting for them, no personal roadies and their cheap instruments keep going out of tune. Yet, every night brings the thrill of performing, fuelled by the hope of catching the audience's eye and perhaps even getting called back for an encore..."Professor" is an interesting, caustic piece that paints in music and words the portrait of an austere, know-it-all man who delights in picking out others' mistakes and point out what an artist is lacking; a ruthless critic who poses as an expert without truly being one. With weary eyes and a black bow tie, he takes pleasure in denigrating the work of others. Yet, one has to wonder: what is the point of dwelling on trivial errors when it would be far more useful to highlight what is actually working? The protagonist is merely a professor who teaches nothing; his petty attitude will ultimately lead him into oblivion, while the people he criticised go on with all their mistakes and their enthusiasm...The last track, "Coffee Song", is a melancholic acoustic ballad about the passing of time and the need to be ready for every new opportunity - despite any despondency or sadness - because there is nothing worse than looking back with regret at having lost the winning path simply because one was tired...On the whole, a very good work.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Goh-Ka by Sigh is another great step forward for the Japanese metal legends, bringing back their earlier more manic Avant Garde black metal and thrash styles and mixing it with their recent folk, melodic and progressive metal sound. More than likely inspired by the re-recording of their classic album Hangman's Hymn, it is a return to parts of their classic sound, but not losing their recent progressive output. As always, Mirai Kawashima's manic vocals are always the unique trademark of the band, and it goes very well with the many different paths this album takes. And some of the melodic guitar work on this is very impressive. I'd give this a high 7 to low 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Kusoshi, 1 2, & 3.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — This short-lived mysterious act that emerged from Pushkin, a nearby suburb of St Petersburg, Russiais the epitome of obscurity having only released its sole effort Литургия безумия / A LITURGY OFMADNESS in 1991 and then never to be heard from again. Given it debuted during the tumultuous timewhen the Soviet Union was collapsing into the Russian Federation and outlying nations, the band andalbum has become a very forgotten entry in the region's rich musical history. This psychedelicprogressive band was the trio of bassist Aleksandr Berezkin, guitarist Aleksey Romanov and drummerIvan Fedenko, the latter of which was a seasoned Soviet musician having played in the new wave actAVIA as well as the jazz fusion ensemble Junglie.Together this triumvirate of instrumental experimental prog crafted an album's worth of complexpsychedelia where classic prog nods effortlessly free flow through an album's worth of psychedelichaze augmented by Beefheart inspired angularities and Pink Floyd infused grooviness. Whiletechnically hosting 13 individual tracks, the album can rightfully be thought of as two side-longtracks that offer variations on a theme to transition from one motif and cadence to the nextoffering moments of high energy rock along with an ever-changing rotisserie of time signatures,tempos, tones and progressive weavings. The album has been cited as catering the melodic prowess ofclassic Yes recordings laced with off-kilter avant-progeny angularities that sprang into existenceat the end of the 1970s but this is very subtle in actuality.Beginning with the raucous ride that constitutes side one, the wily suite "Бешеный Огурец, Часть 1 /Mad Cucumber, Part" displays a fertile musical fecundity in action where essentially a jam bandchannels its inner prog credentials and takes a five-part journey through musical terrains thatemulate past masters but yet sound like none of them. A crafty and creative wild ride through mostlyguitar-driven / keyboard-free excursions through meandering musical motifs, A LITURGY OF MADNESSdespite it's title and insinuations that it will be a dark journey of the soul actually comes off asmore light-hearted and stews in the broth of psychedelia more than the underbelly of the earlyUnivers Zero playbook yet many nods to avant-prog masters of yore insert their angular angles intothe overall context. Some clear King Crimson references also are in the overall fabric.Although some will claim the album is a continuous flow from beginning to end, in reality the firstside is clearly delineated from the second with "Бешеный Огурец, Часть 2 / Mad Cucumber, Part 2"taking on a distinctly different mood setting although in general the same meandering unpredictableprocession of what sounds like aimless musically lollygagging that somehow flows organically andwithout startling unrelated transitions. Despite the avant-prog reference the music is overall moreon the melodic side but creatively distinct as not really pointing to many other bands that hademerged up to this point in the prog timeline. For the most part this is a subtle release thatdoesn't offer a lot in terms of timbres and instrumental offerings with all the creative effortstucked into the varying motifs that span on for a 40 1/2 minute mind journey. This is one that tooka few spins to sink in but ultimately delivers a nice meandering package of highly idiosyncraticpsychedelia that sounds fairly unique.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — In many ways the Russian modern day equivalent of Goblin, the Vladimir (city) based ENINE has carvedout a unique niche in the world of symphonic guitar-driven prog that takes inspiration thematicallyfrom the subject matter of early silent films, patricianly the horror cinema of the 1920s whilemarrying it to the world of 70s symphonic and space rock prog courtesy of bands such as Eloy, PinkFloyd, Camel and Genesis. This band was founded by guitarist Vladimir Mihailov and keyboardist IlyaFrolov who worked together in the prog band Algabas and after adding three more members released alive album "Live In Saint Petersburg" which served as the official debut. This first studio offeringTHE GREAT SILENT followed in 2018 and to this day only one additional album, "Spiritus Natura" hascome to fruition.Living up to the album title, the subject matter is indeed silent horror and sci-fi films thatspanned the 1910s and 1920s. Inspirations are drawn from classics such as "Metropolis (1927)" and"Noseferatu (1922)" as well as "Dr. Caligari (1920)" and "Frankenstein (1910)" all without reallytaking the music into the dark mood settings that such titles would suggest. This all instrumentalalbum features eight tracks (2 of which are lesss than a minute) and offers some nice symphonicspace jamming with some sounding fairly original and others sounding right out of the 70s playbook."Waiting For.." offers a cliche throwback to 70s Pink Floyd for example. The opening "Welcome ToMonochrome" sets the tone for a nonchalant ride through jammy space rock laced with symphonicbombast reminiscent most of 70s Eloy yet the band steers clear of repeating the same idea for toolong. The strongest tracks come at the beginning with "The Curse Of Dr Caligari" which features a Floydianhypnotic bass groove accompanied by fiery Eloy inspired keyboard attacks. The addition of the fluteoffers some nice touches while the bass thumps and the guitar initiates its trickery and likewise"The Light Of Metropolis" offers more of the same albeit with an entirely different melodicunderpinning. However the track lacks the sense of dread that the film conveyed so well. "Workers"is perhaps the closest thing a true dark sounding track with nice fuzzy bass tones but even thisfalls short of what the album cover art portends. "Frankenstein" offers some nice jaw harp andkeyboard wizardry but once again what should be more in the Goblin playbook given the theme comesoff as a rather breezy symphonic walk in the park but does pick up tempo and offers some of the morerockin' moments.The album slightly tapers off in quality towards the end. Overall this was one that made a nicefirst impression but like Morte Macabre and similarly minded acts fails to sustain my interest asthis type of thing has been done so well by Goblin and other horror prog acts. In the end it's apleasure to listen to a couple times but not quite up to par with many of the true darker progclassics whether they be from early Univers Zero or the plethora of darkened zeuhl and avant-progthat kept the 80s underground humming along. Nice keyboard workouts and instrumental workouts and ifyou prefer a much lighter sound for this kind of music then you might be more invigorated by it thani am. Still though, a nice semi-unique offering by a rather unknown band from Russia.

items.body: Review by Stefano61 — There is a particular stretch of English coast, in Yorkshire, where the North Sea arrives already telling stories before it reaches the shore. In 1890 a Dublin theatre manager on holiday there climbed the long run of steps up to the abbey ruins above the harbour, heard the local tale of a storm driven ship that ran aground with its entire crew already dead, and went home to write the most famous shipwreck in English fiction. Bram Stoker never lived in Whitby. He only visited, and the town gave him nightmares he carried for the rest of his career.A century later it gave something gentler, though no less powerful, to a boy who did live there, listening from his bedroom to the same water arriving against the same cliffs in winter. Steve Rothery grew up in Whitby. Decades later, looking for somewhere to begin a record with an old friend, he did not reach for a studio concept. He walked Steve Hackett along that same coast and showed him where it had all started.Between them the two guitarists carry over half a century of British progressive music. Hackett spent the first half of the nineteen seventies inside Genesis, shaping some of that band's most enduring guitar writing before a long, prolific solo career that in 2018 finally let him revisit that early material live, with a full band and orchestra behind him. Rothery has been the sound of Marillion's guitar since the band's earliest days, a voice built less on speed than on sustain, on knowing exactly how long to hold a note before letting it go. The two men had circled each other's orbit for decades without ever actually making a record together, until this one.The Roaring Waves took the better part of a decade to arrive, worked on intermittently between tours and other commitments, in sessions at Rothery's own studio in Buckinghamshire and in both men's homes. Hackett has described the approach as deliberately old fashioned, closer to friends gathering in a garage than to any formal writing session, built from jams and shared ideas rather than material arriving pre written. Rothery, used to working this way from Marillion's own methods, found the looseness familiar. Hackett, whose long collaboration with the Hungarian band Djabe had already taught him something about improvising inside someone else's musical language, took a little longer to settle into it. What both men insisted on, repeatedly, was that neither should try to outplay the other. The record was to paint with sound rather than race across it.They are joined by the Italian musician Riccardo Romano, who plays keyboards and bass, produced and mixed the record, and co wrote three of its seven pieces, alongside drummers Daniele Pomo, across the first five tracks, and Leon Parr, who takes over for the last two. Romano and Pomo already knew Rothery's music from the inside, having played for years in his own solo band, and it shows in how naturally they hold the ground beneath two guitarists who could easily have crowded each other out.Seven instrumental pieces, nothing sung, everything said through guitar, and one subject holding the whole record together: the sea, and everything memory and imagination have ever hung on it. The record does not stay in Yorkshire. It begins there, at the harbour Rothery grew up beside, then drifts outward toward waters that have nothing to do with his childhood at all, a vanished Cold War submarine, a contested inland sea, an American highway running the length of an entirely different ocean, as though one coastline, looked at closely enough, always leads a person back out to every other.- The Storm: the album's overture and its most turbulent piece, opening on Riccardo Romano's simulated strings before Hackett enters with dramatic, almost marching guitar lines, power chords, and Daniele Pomo's drums arriving as though in procession behind him. The two guitarists trade call and response phrases across a vamp stretched taut but never quite breaking, the closest the record comes to outright aggression before the sea, as it always eventually does, calms.- Sandsend: named for the small village just along the coast from Whitby, and the record's first real exhale, its main melody so vocal in shape it could almost be sung. Where The Storm gave the coastline its ferocity, Sandsend gives it wonder, a gentle rise and fall of guitar over patient drumming and understated bass, evoking a childhood spent walking that particular stretch of sand rather than fearing it. Rothery has spoken of the place as somewhere genuinely touched by magic, and the piece carries that without ever needing to say so directly.- Red Dragon: named after a seventeenth century East India Company ship, and the record's most overtly adventurous piece, opening on the drone of a hurdy gurdy, an instrument that reaches back to medieval Europe, before Rothery's riff turns heavy and Hackett answers with sitar guitar and melodic lines chasing an unmistakably Eastern flavour. A d�tour east, briefly, before the record returns to its own coastline.- The Roaring Waves: the title piece, and the record's centre of gravity, opening on Hackett's fingerpicked nylon string guitar before orchestral strings rise beneath a single soaring melody that eventually erupts into a full blooded solo. The two guitarists close it out in genuine duet, before the whole thing settles into an acoustic coda carried by piano, tension gathered and then, finally, allowed to rest.- K-129: named for a Soviet submarine lost in the Pacific in 1968 with its entire crew, its true fate still disputed decades later. The piece opens on a looping, mechanical pulse standing in for the vessel's own repeated motion through the water, ghostly sonar pings drifting through the mix, Rothery's playing staying melodic even as Hackett pushes toward distortion and noise. It is the moment on the record that leans furthest from guitar rock and closest to Rothery's own recent electronic collaborations, nearer Tangerine Dream than Marillion, before the two guitars eventually surface again together.- The Black Sea: the record's slowest, most reflective piece, built on restraint rather than notes played fast, and all the more affecting for it. Depth, isolation, pressure, everything the title promises, delivered through melody rather than volume.- Pacific Coast Highway: the closing piece, and a genuine change of climate, harmonica and quick, bright riffs pulling the record decisively out of its own melancholy and toward something closer to blues rock, fast and warm and, after six pieces built largely on weather and depth, almost startlingly sunlit. An unexpected way to end a record about the sea, and exactly right for it.What makes The Roaring Waves work is not really its instrumental fireworks, though there is no shortage of those, but its refusal to stay in one place. It begins as a very personal record, one man's coastline handed to an old friend as a way of explaining himself, and ends up as something closer to a history of the sea itself, its wrecks, its wars, its holiday postcards.Two guitarists who could easily have spent seven tracks proving who was faster instead spent them listening to each other, and the record is better for the restraint. If it has a fault, it is one earned honestly: built largely from jams rather than pre written songs, the middle stretch occasionally lets atmosphere do work a sharper melodic idea might have done better, and this is a record that rewards patient, attentive listening rather than a single pass in the car.Coming from two men in their sixties and seventies who had never previously made a record together, that patience feels less like a flaw than like the whole point. Whitby gave Bram Stoker a nightmare that outlived him by more than a century. It has now given Steve Hackett and Steve Rothery something gentler and, in its own way, just as lasting. My rating: 4/5.(Bassano del Grappa, Italy, September 2026)

items.body: Review by SeeHatfield — Since Rick Davies' passing I've been on a Supertramp kick, revisiting a band I once loved but lost touch with. Truth to tell, Supertramp was one of my first rock band crushes (after the Beatles). From about 1980 through 1983, I listened to them devotedly, committing their music to memory: every lick, every solo, every detail. Eventually I got to see them on the Famous Last Words tour, at one of their very last shows with Roger Hodgson (per setlist.fm, at the LA Forum between Sept. 22 and 24, 1983). I was ecstatic about that show, though sad to hear about Hodgson's pending exit. That said, it didn't take me long to fall out of love with Famous Last Words, which I knew was not as good as any of the four previous albums. By the mid-80s I had lost interest in the band, telling myself that Supertramp without Hodgson was pointless and that they weren't a spontaneous or exciting live act (a judgment I now think a bit unfair). The incarnation of Supertramp that really matters to me is the classic lineup (Davies, Hodgson, Helliwell, Siebenberg, Thompson) that lasted from mid-1973 through late 1983, and in particular its first four albums (1974-1979). The Davies/Hodgson partnership peaked, I think, with the first of those albums, Crime of the Century (1974). In fact, each succeeding album is a bit less satisfying, the partnership a bit more distant or attenuated -- though I still think Crisis? What Crisis? (1975) and Even in the Quietest Moments (1977) are excellent. Crime of the Century has a wholeness to it that I particularly love. In the roughly two years between the crumbling of the old Supertramp lineup and the birth of this new, definitive one in the summer of 1973, Davies and Hodgson must have been woodshedding like mad. Their writing took a huge leap. All told, about three years separated their previous album from the final release of Crime, and you can tell that the band made the most of its time together. Reportedly, the new lineup spent time living together in 1973-1974 and rehearsing nonstop to refine its new songs. The result was a set of polished, deliberately arranged numbers worked out by the band before recording. Supertramp had never done anything remotely like this before -- this was, essentially, a new start. And the sound! I'm not much of an audiophile or headphones listener, but Crime of the Century is a sonically brilliant album, full of evocative sound images. Often, these images suggest a full, even cavernous space, with Davies or Hodgson singing from far off, then coming closer, as the songs surge and then overwhelm the listener. Co-producer Ken Scott helps make the record an immersive 3D soundscape. Impeccable production flourishes are everywhere: from the sepulchral harmonica that opens the album, to the way the dying last note of "School" becomes the thumping first note of "Bloody Well Right," to the multitracked vocals, twinned keyboards, and odd sounds. Dig that ghostly, theremin- (or musical saw?) like counterpoint in "Hide In Your Shell"; the equally spooky, distant voicings in "Dreamer"; or the thrumming, insistent string chart in "Rudy." It's all transporting. None of that would matter if the album didn't contain the strongest set of songs Davies and Hodgson ever worked up together. The writing justifies everything else. That was the thing about Supertramp: they weren't driven by outsized personalities, a magnetic frontman, or even their considerable chops. They were driven by songs, and often they worked those songs to perfection. The album begins and ends with songs that, lyrically, are simple and spare. Hodgson's haunted "School" and Davies' acrid "Bloody Well Right" consist of just a few succinct verses -- in fact, the latter is nearly skeletal, no more than a couple of stanzas. Ditto the album's closer, "Crime of the Century," which runs to about a dozen lines. Yet each of these songs is made complete by lengthy, painstakingly arranged instrumentals -- not jamming, but instrumental writing that is integral to the songs. "School" builds and builds, eerily, then spins out into a keyboard solo; "Bloody Well Right" starts with a lengthy keyboard solo, then resolves into a crunchy, bluesy riff and snarling guitar fills. The title track, famously, is all simplicity and space, Davies singing the brief lyric as if from far away, followed by Hodgson's pained, double-tracked guitar solo, and then, at the two-minute mark, Davies' hypnotically simple, repeating piano figure. That spartan piano riff carries the number away, off into the deep distance, in a fadeout that runs more than three minutes, flavored by Bob Siebenberg's slow, almost narcotized, yet brilliant drum fills. There's a heaviness to it that has nothing to do with "hard rock."The in-between tracks on the album include three slow-building mini-epics, "Hide In Your Shell," "Asylum," and "Rudy." Each of these is tuneful, singable, accessible, and yet has an unconventional shape (for a pop song), with, again, discrete sections and a gathering momentum. "Hide In Your Shell" cycles twice through the same buildup, from gentle to frantic, then climaxes in an odd section that upshifts from a low, throbbing pulse (I want to know you) to Hodgson's final desperate vocal outburst (Oh, we're such damn fools). "Asylum," similarly, cycles twice through a complex structure, building from laidback cynicism to theatrical screwiness, then climaxes with Davies hollering insanely. "Rudy," the album's masterstroke, dispenses with familiar verse/chorus form altogether and has a climactic break that accelerates like the train that Rudy's on, while Hodgson and Davies trade call-and-response vocals (All through your life / All through the years). Its finale is like a brilliant trainwreck.What I most love about these odd songs is the fact that Davies and Hodgson sing them together. Yes, I know that the shared songwriting in Supertramp was typically a matter of parallel play rather than full collaboration, and I know that each song is carried by the voice of its writer. But it's heartening to hear the two singer-songwriters working together on these tracks, each striving to lift the other's songs to full flight. They would never again sing so much in support of each other. Hodgson's keening tenor (and doomy guitar) fill out Davies' songs; Davies' raw baritone contrasts nicely with Hodgson's angelic highs. Meanwhile, the layered keyboards, contributed by both of them, make everything cohere. The shared singing and playing suggest a partnership that was already at its zenith. More good -- very good -- albums would follow, but Crime of the Century was the band's essential moment of reinvention, self-discovery, and peak collaboration. From there, Davies and Hodgson would learn about their differences, and ever so slowly pull away. RIP Rick Davies (1944-2025). I originally wrote this review soon after his passing.

items.body: Review by SeeHatfield — Is hate-listening a thing? On a whim, I decided to listen to Tales of Mystery and Imagination for perhaps the first time ever, or at least the first in some forty years (a college friend and roommate may have had it, back in the mid-Eighties). I have never been a fan of the Alan Parsons Project, and upon listening to it, just the other night, I mean really listening to it, all the way through, I remain a non-fan.To tell the truth, I started railing against the album while still in midstream. What pleasure I got from it came from my daughter, sitting next to me, who cackled while listening. Cackled, but then occasionally roared. It's that bad.The album is a chestnut, something that was already out of tune with the times in 1976. It's the sort of thing that happens when you "do" prog without either the fire and sensibility of a brilliant singer-songwriter or the chemistry of a live band determined to shoot the works. Basically, it combines slick, studio-bred mid-Seventies pop with the ersatz theatrics of a lesser Andrew Lloyd Webber rock opera. Driven by the meticulous producer/engineer Parsons and his songwriter and arranging partner Eric Woolfson ("executive producer"), it's a long, soporific sleepwalk enlivened only by moments of grandstanding cheesiness, for example the vocal histrionics of Arthur Brown (!) and Leonard Whiting. Looping keyboards dominate, providing the basic rhythms for most everything else, though moments of pounding rock try to add drama. Oy.Lots of talent and many names were drafted into this project. Orchestrator Andrew Powell does a lot of work, as do players from the bands Ambrosia and Pilot. Incredibly, even Curved Air alum Francis Monkman lends a hand. That doesn't help. The songwriting is thin and cliched, though the glistening studio craft strains to compensate. "The Raven" and "The Tell-Tale Heart" are so over the top that they conjure Meat Loaf or Rocky Horror (I dig Rocky Horror, BTW, but that's something else). "The Fall of the House of Usher," a 15-minute suite that dominated Side 2 of the original vinyl release, is a lushly arranged yet torpid instrumental that strives to build to a climactic "fall" but doesn't stick the landing. Beyond the slick playing and atmospheric seamlessness of the recording, there's little happening here. Compositionally, it's a flat graph. The songs fail to conjure either the contemplative or morbid moods that the Poe conceit calls for; there's little of the Gothic intensity of, say, The Strawbs or Peter Hammill at their most intense. Instead, it's all about polish and "skill" (yawn). Suffice to say that this fabled album has done nothing to change the basic impression I got so long ago from APP hits like "Games People Play," "Time," and "Eye in the Sky." None of those songs ever did anything for me, and this record doesn't either. The music is glitzy, the writing lacks bite, and the singing badly wants a dose of eccentricity and warmth. This is somewhere between telethon music and stagy excess, but, to my ears, middling, unchallenging, and fatally lacking in edge.Clearly, this isn't the "band" for me. I'll spare you all any future APP reviews!(For the record, the version I listened to was the 1987 remix with added narration by Orson Welles. Didn't help.)

items.body: Review by SeeHatfield — I know next to nothing about the history of PFM (apart from what I've read here on Prog Archives and on Wikipedia), and I couldn't name the band's members without referencing a cheat sheet. I usually don't have any idea of what they're singing about, either. But I've been listening to them on and off for the better part of forty years, and I know their first five studio albums (plus the English-language adaptations of two of them). I thank a prog-loving friend for making me a tape of Storia Di Un Minuto and its follow-up, Per Un Amico, back in my undergrad days; those two albums in particular cast a spell on me.Without ever researching the lyrics or the band, I came to love those two records (even as I somehow lost or ditched my copy of the English-language Photos of Ghosts along the way). I've come to realize that I greatly prefer the very early PFM, when it included flautist and violinist Mauro Pagani and did not yet include vocalist Bernardo Lanzetti. I think those were the prime years.Storia Di Un Minuto must surely count as one of the great debuts in progressive rock. It's tuneful, inventive, dynamic, and fun, channeling obvious Crimso and Tull influences in the direction of richly melodic, romantic Italianicity. It's eminently hummable, an album of great themes and fragments, with so many moments that stick in my mind. I won't go into detail, but must note that this is exactly what I like about vintage prog: the feeling of several musicians putting their heads and hands together and treating the studio like a laboratory. There's a lot of skill in these five players, but more important than their chops is their enthusiasm for raiding the rag basket, stitching together so many disparate elements, and pushing themselves past their limits. There's a shamelessness about this kind of music, and a sheer love of discovery. Storia Di Un Minuto, at just under 35 minutes, is so full of good stuff that it's a bit of a miracle."Impressioni di Settembre," with its upward-straining melodic hook at the end of each verse (that lovely upsurge of mellotron and Moog), is PFM's "Crimson King," while "La Carrozza di Hans" weds Tullish flute to a frantic, "Schizoid Man"-style 6/8 section and, "Aqualung"-style, jams together different bits into a frantic musical puzzle. These moves are familiar, but with PFM the delight is the distinctiveness of their own melodies. Also, the singing, though divvied up among several members, is good throughout (I've never thought of Lanzetti as an improvement). In a few years, PFM would crank up the heavy rock, bank on their skill, and lose some of their early delicacy (listen to the virtuosic hammering of Chocolate Kings to know what I mean). I think that's too bad. The good stuff was the exploratory early stuff, which happened to birth some excellent songs and lovely scraps. Maybe I should figure out the lyrics now?

items.excerpt: FiXT releases Scandroid’s cover of Celldweller’s “Jericho” on 9 September 2026 as a digital single, the second transmission from Klayton’s upcoming Scandroid album “Lost Horizon.” The cover reworks the original into a fusion of post-punk, gothic rock and retro-futuristic synthwave, pairing synthesizers and heavy guitars with driving rhythms and a cinematic atmosphere. Jericho by Scandroid “My next single is a Scandroid cover of Celldweller’s
items.body: FiXT releases Scandroid’s cover of Celldweller’s “Jericho” on 9 September 2026 as a digital single, the second transmission from Klayton’s upcoming Scandroid album “Lost Horizon.” The cover reworks the original into a fusion of post-punk, gothic rock and retro-futuristic synthwave, pairing synthesizers and heavy guitars with driving rhythms and a cinematic atmosphere. Jericho by Scandroid “My next single is a Scandroid cover of Celldweller’s ‘Jericho.’ I wanted to approach this song by mashing retro styles I loved, like punk, post-punk, and new wave into something that is clearly and uniquely different from the original Celldweller version of the song,” Klayton stated. Klayton wrote and produced “Jericho,” with Joel Wanasek mixing the track and Maor Appelbaum handling mastering; Cory Todd created the cover art, and Celldweller Music holds the publishing credit. The original “Jericho” appeared on Celldweller‘s 2015 album “End of an Empire.” Celldweller most recently released the single “Respawn” from the forthcoming album “GOD MODE.” Scandroid released an accompanying lyric video for “Jericho” on YouTube, and the single streams on Spotify and other major platforms. “Jericho” follows May 2026’s “Lost in the Stars” as the second transmission from “Lost Horizon,” Klayton’s fourth Scandroid studio album, set in the year 2525. A world-building novella by authors Joshua Viola and Sean Eads accompanies the album, alongside planned physical formats including Mini-Disc, cassette, CD and vinyl; “Lost Horizon” is expected in 2027. FiXT also offers a “Lost Horizon” season pass on EVEN, with bonus tracks and early access to further singles ahead of the full album. About Scandroid Klayton, an artist and producer from Detroit, Michigan, best known for his Celldweller project, launched Scandroid in 2013 together with producer Varien (Nick Pittsinger), releasing the debut single “Salvation Code” on 6 August 2013 and the single “Datastream” that December. Varien left the project in August 2014 to focus on his own music, leaving Klayton as Scandroid’s sole member. The self-titled debut album, “Scandroid,” followed on 11 November 2016 and reached No. 20 on the Billboard Heatseekers Albums chart and No. 5 on the Top Dance/Electronic Albums chart; Side-Line reviewed the album on its CD release. The remix collection “Dreams of Neo-Tokyo” arrived in March 2017, followed by the second Scandroid album, “Monochrome”, on 27 October 2017, which reached No. 18 on Heatseekers and No. 3 on the Top Dance/Electronic Album Sales chart. Klayton released the EPs “The Darkness” (2018) and “The Light” (2019), combining them into the double album “The Darkness and the Light” in December 2020, followed by the remix collection “Dreams of Darkness, Visions of Light” in November 2021. Scandroid is one of several outlets for Klayton’s music alongside Celldweller, Circle of Dust and FreqGen. Scandroid returned in May 2026 with the single “Lost in the Stars,” the first transmission from the planned fourth studio album “Lost Horizon,” and now follows it with “Jericho,” the second transmission from that album, out now on FiXT, the label Klayton co-founded with James Rhodes in 2006.

items.body: Finnish Electronic Punk duo I Think I Broke Something releases the single “Heads Up” on September 9. The track is the second single from the duo’s upcoming EP “Another Escape,” due November 5 on the same day as a release show at Semifinal in Helsinki. Heads Up by I Think I Broke Something “Heads Up is our take on an accessible dance track. It’s a pretty straightforward rave/electropunk/industrial stomper with too much distortion. There might be a hint of irony in the lyrics,” the band states. ‘Heads Up’ follows ‘Illegal’ toward ‘Another Escape’ “Heads Up” arrives a month after “Illegal,” the first single from “Another Escape.” Both tracks lead into the EP, out November 5, with the band marking the release the same day with a show at Semifinal in Helsinki. The duo places its sound somewhere between The Prodigy, 3TEETH and Nine Inch Nails, and lists collaborations with The Prodigy’s Maxim, DJ Hyper and Zardonic. About I Think I Broke Something I Think I Broke Something, also known as ITIBS, is a Helsinki-based duo made up of Jouni and Miika, active since 2014. The project debuted with the EP “Superman Sabotage Clan” and has since released three full-length albums, including “Still Not Going To” on October 26, 2022, alongside numerous singles and remixes through various labels. Prior singles included “Astral”, “Corpse” and “Raw”, the latter remixed by drum’n’bass and metal producer Zardonic; the duo has also worked with The Prodigy’s Maxim and DJ Hyper. ITIBS describes its sound as a distorted electronic hybrid drawing on The Prodigy, Skinny Puppy and 3TEETH, mixing explosive electronics with metal-heavy weight. “Heads Up,” released September 9, follows “Illegal” as the second single from the EP “Another Escape,” due November 5 alongside the band’s release show at Semifinal in Helsinki.

items.album: Liars announce new album ‘A Ban On Plastic Bag Bans’, out 5 March 2027 on Mute
